options.text: Relationships replace every need for character
Only solitary decisions can develop virtue
Relationships can help cultivate habitual integrity and good judgement
Learning is relevant only to technical skill

questions.explanation: The deck links good character with learning and building business relationships.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 2 deck; slide 2

questions.stem: Why should competitiveness not be equated with virtue?

options.text: Commercial effectiveness and moral character are different qualities
Every successful business trait is automatically a moral virtue
Competitive firms cannot have any integrity
A lack of competitors proves a person is virtuous

questions.explanation: The slides distinguish toughness and competitiveness from virtues such as compassion and truthfulness.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 2 deck; slide 1

questions.stem: Which response best recognises culture without abandoning judgement in virtue ethics?

options.text: Ignore culture and all relationships
Consider context while critically judging how virtues should guide conduct
Assume every local habit is virtuous because it is common
Replace judgement with the highest immediate profit

questions.explanation: The approach acknowledges community ideals but still needs knowledge and judgement in applying traits.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 2 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: Virtue ethics places its central emphasis on:

options.text: The cultivation of character through recurring patterns of conduct.
The enforceability of a contract as the sole test of good conduct.
The likelihood that an action will escape punishment.
The net consequences of each isolated act as the only moral criterion.
The satisfaction of whatever preferences a person happens to have.

questions.explanation: Virtue ethics focuses on cultivated character and recurring conduct, rather than reducing morality to the result of an isolated act.
questions.source: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 2 — Virtue Ethics (https://app.notion.com/p/6713c6a92a1848108baa9a86101d3855)

questions.stem: Which ONE pair most clearly represents moral virtues, rather than commercial toughness or performance measures alone?

options.text: Integrity and compassion.
Ambition and bargaining power.
Visibility and popularity.
Aggressiveness and dominance.
Market share and sales growth.

questions.explanation: Integrity and compassion are moral qualities, whereas market share and dominance are not themselves sufficient evidence of virtue.
questions.source: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 2 — Virtue Ethics (https://app.notion.com/p/6713c6a92a1848108baa9a86101d3855)

questions.stem: A code praises courage and honesty but gives little guidance about how to choose between two conflicting obligations. Which ONE limitation of virtue ethics does this illustrate?

options.text: Identifying desirable character traits may not provide a precise decision procedure for every case.
A virtuous person must give identical answers to every moral dilemma.
An action has moral worth only when it is required by an employment contract.
Virtue ethics is concerned only with financial outcomes.
Character cannot be developed through repeated behaviour.

questions.explanation: A list of virtues can orient judgement without providing an exact procedure for resolving every difficult choice.
questions.source: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 2 — Virtue Ethics (https://app.notion.com/p/6713c6a92a1848108baa9a86101d3855)

chapters.title: Week 5.3 — Rights, Justice & Moral Dialogue
chapters.description: Rights, Rawls, inclusive discourse, pluralism and resolving disagreement.

questions.stem: Which obligation corresponds most directly to a right to be left alone?

options.text: Maximise the other person’s utility by force
Provide a particular cash benefit in every case
Ignore the person’s choices
Do not interfere without justification

questions.explanation: The deck connects this right with an obligation of non-interference.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 1

questions.stem: Why can the responsibility for a positive right be disputed in business?

options.text: The existence of a right automatically names one provider in every case
It may be unclear whether the state or private companies should provide the relevant benefit
Rights never imply any duty
Only individuals can bear any obligation

questions.explanation: The deck asks whose responsibility provision should be.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 2

questions.stem: What is a key difficulty when several rights conflict?

options.text: Rights always rank in alphabetical order
The theory does not supply a clear hierarchy resolving every conflict
Conflicting rights are impossible by definition
The right with the highest financial return always prevails

questions.explanation: The slide notes the absence of a clear methodology and hierarchy.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 2

questions.stem: Why might rights theories appeal to a multinational?

options.text: They guarantee that every culture interprets every right identically
They make local law irrelevant
They remove the need to investigate human-rights exposure
They can offer transnational and transcultural ethical norms

questions.explanation: The deck describes cross-border norms as attractive while acknowledging theoretical limitations.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 2

questions.stem: What priority does the Rawls slide assign to equal basic liberty?

options.text: Priority only when aggregate profits rise
Priority over economic policy
No priority when a majority dislikes it
A secondary role after all productivity goals

questions.explanation: The slide states that equal liberty takes priority over economic policy.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: Which policy best fits the slide’s emphasis on fair equality of opportunity?

options.text: Offer identical job titles but deny disadvantaged applicants training
Choose candidates only by family wealth
Make positions accessible with necessary training rather than merely declaring them open
Reserve all positions for the already advantaged

questions.explanation: The slide explicitly links opportunity with access to positions and necessary training.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: What does ideal versus non-ideal theory help a decision-maker do?

options.text: Ignore the needs of differently-abled citizens
Assume the current system is already perfectly fair
Compare fair arrangements with current conditions and consider improvements
Choose policy without identifying any standard

questions.explanation: The slides describe setting out an ideal and considering departures and remedies.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 3

questions.stem: Why is stakeholder participation a practical limitation for discourse ethics?

options.text: Only shareholders count as relevant participants
Excluding affected groups automatically improves moral legitimacy
Consensus can never require any time
Reaching consensus can take time and depends on relevant stakeholders being able to participate

questions.explanation: The deck lists time and participation by all relevant stakeholders as difficulties.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 4

questions.stem: In the Bauman presentation, why should decision-makers interact with affected people?

options.text: To make professional norms independent of personal convictions
To substitute publicity for ethical reflection
To avoid distance from moral situations and develop an informed personal moral sense
To establish that universal codes have been scientifically proved impossible

questions.explanation: The slide advocates local interaction and learning; it presents Bauman’s theoretical position rather than a universal proven fact.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 5

questions.stem: Two teams disagree about fairness but use different meanings of the term. What should they do first?

options.text: Let the most powerful team define the term privately
Vote before identifying what each team means
Clarify definitions before assuming the conflict is fundamentally moral
Ignore definitions and compare budgets only

questions.explanation: The deck notes that apparent moral disagreement may be conceptual.
questions.source: MG2008 current 2026–27 Week 5 Part 3 deck; slide 6

questions.stem: Which ONE statement correctly distinguishes positive from negative rights?

options.text: Positive rights are always legally enforceable; negative rights are always voluntary.
Positive rights belong to employees; negative rights belong to employers.
Positive rights concern money; negative rights can never create obligations.
Positive rights require provision or action; negative rights require non-interference.
Positive rights are moral claims; negative rights are necessarily unlawful claims.

questions.explanation: Positive rights call for action or provision, while negative rights call for others to refrain from interference. Both can imply duties.
questions.source: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences (https://app.notion.com/p/832fa2528ec247fe95d9773986774731)

questions.stem: What is the purpose of Rawls’s original-position and veil-of-ignorance exercise?

options.text: To choose principles without knowing the social position one will occupy.
To eliminate every possible difference in personal outcomes.
To choose principles after confirming that one will belong to the wealthiest group.
To choose principles using only the preferences of existing property owners.
To replace equal liberties with whichever allocation produces the highest GDP.

questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance removes knowledge of one’s eventual social position so that principles are not chosen simply to favour a known personal advantage.
questions.source: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences (https://app.notion.com/p/832fa2528ec247fe95d9773986774731); Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58) (https://app.notion.com/p/d61a87e18e554146a2931313adc789dd)

questions.stem: Which ONE policy justification is LEAST consistent with the difference principle as discussed in the module?

options.text: A proposed inequality should be assessed partly by its implications for the least advantaged.
Assessing inequality requires more than identifying who produces the largest private return.
The distribution of gains matters, not merely the size of the total gain.
Equal division of every reward is not the only conceivable just arrangement.
An inequality is justified simply because total output rises, even though the least advantaged receive no benefit.

questions.explanation: The difference principle cannot justify inequality merely by pointing to aggregate growth while the least advantaged receive no benefit.
questions.source: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences (https://app.notion.com/p/832fa2528ec247fe95d9773986774731); Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58) (https://app.notion.com/p/d61a87e18e554146a2931313adc789dd)

questions.stem: A stakeholder consultation allows the largest investor to determine the outcome while affected residents cannot meaningfully participate. Which ONE concern is most relevant to discourse ethics?

options.text: Dialogue is ethically satisfactory once the most powerful party agrees.
Consensus requires excluding participants whose concerns are difficult to measure.
The process should consider only stakeholders with contractual voting rights.
The conditions for genuine dialogue are undermined when power dominates participation.
Participation removes the need to give reasons for a decision.

questions.explanation: Discourse ethics requires meaningful participation and reason-giving; domination by power undermines the conditions of genuine dialogue.
questions.source: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences (https://app.notion.com/p/832fa2528ec247fe95d9773986774731)

questions.stem: Which option gives the COMPLETE set of useful steps for resolving moral disagreements in the lecture? (i) Clarify disputed facts; (ii) clarify the meanings of important terms; (iii) test whether the reasoning is consistent.

options.text: (i) only.
(ii) and (iii) only.
(i) and (ii) only.
(i), (ii) and (iii).
(i) and (iii) only.

questions.explanation: Clarifying facts, meanings and consistency addresses different sources of disagreement, so all three steps are relevant.
questions.source: [CURRENT 2026–27] Week 5, Part 3 — Rights Theories, Discourse Ethics and Resolving Moral Differences (https://app.notion.com/p/832fa2528ec247fe95d9773986774731)

chapters.title: Week 6.1 — Stakeholders & Corporate Purpose
chapters.description: Lecture 6: corporate characteristics, stakeholder approaches and power–interest prioritisation.

questions.stem: A person works for a company, owns some shares and buys its products. How should their stakeholder position be understood?

options.text: Their employment role disappears when they buy a product
They cannot be a stakeholder because the roles overlap
One person may occupy several stakeholder roles
They must be assigned only the shareholder role

questions.explanation: Stakeholder roles can overlap rather than forming mutually exclusive identities.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: What is the central challenge stakeholder theory poses to a profit-only view of corporate purpose?

options.text: Business responsibilities extend to relevant stakeholders beyond shareholders
Shareholders must never be considered
Only groups with direct contracts have moral interests
Every stakeholder must receive exactly the same payment

questions.explanation: The theory broadens the consideration of corporate responsibilities without making every interest identical.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: Which principle matches the corporate-rights aspect of the stakeholder approach?

options.text: A corporation should not violate the rights of others
Rights matter only when they increase immediate profit
A corporation acquires every stakeholder’s rights
Only majority shareholders can possess rights

questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes respecting others’ rights from considering the effects of corporate actions.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: Which principle matches the corporate-effect aspect of the stakeholder approach?

options.text: Only effects named in a sales contract can count
A corporation should take responsibility for the effects of its actions on others
A corporation is responsible only for its share-price graph
Effects on non-customers are automatically irrelevant

questions.explanation: The approach asks firms to consider the consequences of their activities for others.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: A firm checks direct suppliers but ignores serious effects further along the supply network. What does network-oriented stakeholder analysis suggest?

options.text: Only the first supplier can ever be a stakeholder
A supply chain eliminates the need for ethical analysis
Indirectly affected people cannot have interests
Relevant interests can extend beyond immediate contractual partners

questions.explanation: Stakeholder networks can reach through suppliers and other linked actors.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: Which question represents a descriptive stakeholder approach?

options.text: Which stakeholder strategy maximises profit?
Why do stakeholders deserve consideration in their own right?
How can a firm avoid identifying stakeholders?
Who are the stakeholders, and what interests do they have?

questions.explanation: The descriptive approach identifies and describes stakeholders and their interests.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: Why should the label normative stakeholder category not be confused with normative stakeholder theory?

options.text: Both labels mean only shareholders
The category identifies everyone with low interest
The theory is simply a list of media outlets
The category classifies groups such as peer associations; the theory concerns ethical justification

questions.explanation: The lecture uses normative in two distinct classification contexts.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: A stakeholder has high power and high interest in a project. What is the usual power–interest matrix approach?

options.text: Treat as automatically irrelevant
Manage closely
Monitor with minimal engagement only
Keep uninformed

questions.explanation: High-power, high-interest stakeholders generally require close management and engagement.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: A stakeholder has high power but currently low interest. What approach fits the power–interest matrix?

options.text: Use the low-power, high-interest strategy without considering their power
Keep satisfied
Ignore completely
Assume they have no influence

questions.explanation: The matrix recommends keeping high-power, low-interest stakeholders satisfied.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: A community group has low formal power but high interest. What approach fits the matrix while respecting stakeholder ethics?

options.text: Keep informed and consider its interests rather than dismissing them
Ignore it because low power means no moral worth
Transfer its interests to shareholders without consultation
Assume it must control every decision

questions.explanation: The usual strategy is to keep it informed; power is not a measure of intrinsic ethical worth.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: Why should a stakeholder priority map be revisited rather than treated as permanent?

options.text: Only the number of shares can ever change priority
Power, interest and urgency can change as circumstances develop
All stakeholder interests disappear after the first meeting
The map guarantees that no conflict can arise

questions.explanation: Stakeholder management is dynamic; an initial assessment can become outdated.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6, 13 October 2026 — delivered material and transcript

questions.stem: Which ONE statement about shareholders and stakeholders is TRUE?

options.text: Stakeholders include only people with written contracts with the business.
Shareholders cease to be stakeholders when a firm adopts a stakeholder approach.
The terms are interchangeable because only share ownership creates a business interest.
Shareholders are one stakeholder group, but stakeholders also include other groups that affect or are affected by the business.
Stakeholders include only groups that can impose a financial loss on the business.

questions.explanation: Stakeholders include groups that affect or are affected by a business; shareholders are one such group, not the entire category.
questions.source: Lecture 6 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81c2bfe7cdcb0807f5aa); Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) (https://app.notion.com/p/13887a7ef2e74bb5b5408a63c25fb373)

questions.stem: In the stakeholder classification used in the assigned textbook, legislatures, regulators and boards are examples of:

options.text: Functional output stakeholders.
Enabling stakeholders.
Functional input stakeholders.
Diffused stakeholders.
Normative stakeholders.

questions.explanation: In the assigned textbook’s classification, enabling stakeholders include regulators, legislatures and boards because of their authority or ability to enable operations.
questions.source: Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) (https://app.notion.com/p/13887a7ef2e74bb5b5408a63c25fb373) — Textbook pp. 75–76.

questions.stem: In the stakeholder classification used in OpenStax Business Ethics (2018), competitors and industry peers that influence shared standards are examples of:

options.text: Enabling stakeholders.
Functional input stakeholders.
Functional output stakeholders.
Normative stakeholders.
Diffused stakeholders.

questions.explanation: The textbook uses normative stakeholders for peers and competitors influencing shared norms. This category is distinct from the normative approach to stakeholder ethics.
questions.source: Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) (https://app.notion.com/p/13887a7ef2e74bb5b5408a63c25fb373) — Textbook pp. 75–76; this category is distinct from the normative approach to stakeholder management.

questions.stem: Which ONE pairing correctly identifies functional input and functional output stakeholders?

options.text: Inputs: voters and community campaigners; outputs: regulators and boards.
Inputs: employees and suppliers; outputs: customers and distributors.
Inputs: customers and retailers; outputs: employees and suppliers.
Inputs: regulators and legislatures; outputs: boards and shareholders.
Inputs: news media and NGOs; outputs: competitors and industry peers.

questions.explanation: Employees and suppliers contribute inputs; customers and distributors are connected with outputs. These are two sides of the functional category.
questions.source: Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) (https://app.notion.com/p/13887a7ef2e74bb5b5408a63c25fb373) — Textbook pp. 75–76.

questions.stem: Which ONE group best fits the textbook’s “diffused” stakeholder category?

options.text: Regulators authorising the company’s operations.
Customers purchasing the company’s outputs.
Employees providing labour under contract.
Industry peers influencing shared professional norms.
NGOs and news media with an indirect connection to the company.

questions.explanation: Diffused stakeholders have indirect relationships, such as media or NGOs, rather than supplying inputs, buying outputs or exercising formal enabling authority.
questions.source: Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) (https://app.notion.com/p/13887a7ef2e74bb5b5408a63c25fb373)

questions.stem: A company listens to residents only when managers expect a campaign to threaten profits. Which ONE approach to stakeholder management does this most closely represent?

options.text: Virtue-based: the decision is explained solely by the managers’ cultivated character.
Descriptive: the company merely records stakeholder relationships without using them in decisions.
Kantian: managers disregard every consequence when deciding whom to consult.
Instrumental: stakeholder attention is linked to its expected effect on business outcomes.
Normative: residents’ interests are recognised as intrinsically important regardless of profit.

questions.explanation: An instrumental approach responds to stakeholders through expected business consequences. The scenario makes profit impact the condition for attention.
questions.source: Lecture 6 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81c2bfe7cdcb0807f5aa); Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) (https://app.notion.com/p/13887a7ef2e74bb5b5408a63c25fb373)

questions.stem: A firm addresses a small group’s legitimate concern even though the group cannot damage the firm’s financial position. The reason given is that those affected deserve fair consideration in their own right. Which ONE approach is this?

options.text: A shareholder-only allocation model.
The instrumental stakeholder approach.
A purely descriptive stakeholder model.
The normative stakeholder approach.
Short-term ethical egoism.

questions.explanation: The normative approach recognises stakeholders’ intrinsic claims, rather than treating attention only as a means to commercial gain.
questions.source: Lecture 6 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81c2bfe7cdcb0807f5aa); Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) (https://app.notion.com/p/13887a7ef2e74bb5b5408a63c25fb373)

chapters.title: Week 6.2 — Governance & Protected Disclosures
chapters.description: Lecture 6: board and management roles, workplace-resolution bodies and careful recognition of protected disclosures.

questions.stem: Which distinction best describes the board and CEO roles presented in governance teaching?

options.text: The board provides direction and oversight; the CEO leads implementation
The CEO alone sets every governance constraint and oversees themselves
The CEO provides independent oversight of the board while the board handles daily operations
The board and CEO have no distinguishable responsibilities

questions.explanation: Governance separates strategic direction and oversight from day-to-day executive implementation.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What does separate legal personality mean for an incorporated company?

options.text: The company and every shareholder are always the same legal person
The company has legal personality only while its original members remain
Every employee becomes personally identical to the company
The company is a legal entity distinct from its members

questions.explanation: Separate personality distinguishes the corporate entity from the people involved in it.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What does perpetual succession describe in corporate characteristics?

options.text: The original shareholders must remain for the company to continue
Any change in shareholders automatically ends the company
The company can never be wound up
The company can continue despite changes in its membership

questions.explanation: Changes among members do not by themselves end the company’s existence; this does not mean it can never be dissolved.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which description best fits the basic limited-liability characteristic taught for shareholders?

options.text: All shareholders must personally pay every corporate liability without limit
Shareholder exposure is generally limited by their investment or unpaid amount on shares, rather than every corporate debt automatically becoming a personal debt
Shareholders can never lose their investment
Company debts cease to exist when shares are issued

questions.explanation: Limited liability concerns shareholder exposure; it does not mean the business has no debts or risks.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which statement best reflects the lecture’s business-judgement discussion?

options.text: Every decision must maximise this week’s revenue
Directors are prohibited from considering any affected community
Good-faith managerial discretion can allow consideration of business context beyond immediate profit
Managers have unrestricted immunity for fraud

questions.explanation: The teaching examples challenge an absolute profit-only reading; discretion is not unlimited or a defence of fraud.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: How should the US corporate-purpose cases discussed in the lecture be used in an Irish-focused ethics question bank?

options.text: As guarantees that every manager will win any lawsuit
As teaching examples illustrating tensions, not as automatic statements of Irish law
As legislation that directly replaces all Irish company law
As proof that every corporation must ignore stakeholders

questions.explanation: The cases support conceptual discussion; jurisdiction-specific legal claims need separate verification.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: What does a prima facie assessment of a report establish?

options.text: A provisional initial basis for considering the case, not a final finding that wrongdoing is proved
An automatic final criminal conviction
That no investigation is needed
That confidentiality removes the need to assess the report

questions.explanation: The initial assessment is preliminary and must not be confused with a completed determination.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Why distinguish a reasonably mistaken report from a knowingly false allegation?

options.text: Reasonable belief is not the same as deliberate fabrication
Every mistaken detail proves deliberate dishonesty
Only reports supported by a final court judgment can be made
A knowingly false allegation becomes reasonable whenever it is repeated

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasises the belief basis of a report; an error discovered later is not automatically knowing falsity.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6 — delivered material and governance slide summary

questions.stem: Which ONE statement about the sources of Irish corporate governance best reflects the supplied deck?

options.text: Corporate governance consists only of informal preferences expressed by the board.
Governance codes and Acts of the Oireachtas always have identical binding force.
A shareholder agreement replaces every statutory duty applying to the company.
Company law, regulation, largely non-binding codes, constitutions and shareholder agreements can all contribute.
Only stock-exchange rules can impose governance requirements on Irish companies.

questions.explanation: The supplied governance account draws on several sources with different legal force. Non-binding codes are not identical to Acts.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slide 1; a course-source question, not current legal advice.

questions.stem: According to the supplied deck, which ONE combination most closely describes a protected disclosure?

options.text: Any personal disagreement reported publicly, regardless of its work context or content.
A complaint that qualifies solely because the employer disputes it.
Any statement made anonymously, regardless of reasonable belief or reporting conditions.
Information reasonably believed to show relevant wrongdoing, acquired in a work-related context and disclosed through the specified manner.
An allegation that is protected only after the worker obtains a criminal conviction.

questions.explanation: The deck combines reasonable belief, relevant wrongdoing, a work-related context and specified reporting conditions; none of these is replaced simply by publicity or anonymity.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slides 5 and 9.

questions.stem: Which ONE matter would generally be directed to an internal grievance procedure rather than treated as relevant wrongdoing solely on the facts given?

options.text: Information reasonably believed to show a criminal offence in a work-related context.
An interpersonal conflict between a worker and another colleague.
A reasonably believed risk to the health and safety of workers.
Information suggesting the concealment of evidence of relevant wrongdoing.
Information about damage to the environment acquired through work.

questions.explanation: The deck generally distinguishes interpersonal grievances from reports of relevant wrongdoing. A personal conflict alone does not establish a protected disclosure.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slide 5; the wording is “generally”, not an absolute exclusion of every possible workplace dispute.

questions.stem: A worker has work-related information about a serious safety risk likely to occur in the future. Which ONE statement is consistent with the deck?

options.text: Only past wrongdoing can be reported through the protected-disclosure framework.
Health and safety risks qualify only when environmental damage has already occurred.
Likely future wrongdoing can fall within the listed categories; a completed injury is not always required.
A report can qualify only if the worker has personally suffered the predicted injury.
The reporting route becomes irrelevant whenever a future risk is serious.

questions.explanation: The deck includes likely future wrongdoing among the matters that may be reported; it does not always require completed injury.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slide 5.

questions.stem: Under the protected-disclosure framework in the supplied deck, which option gives the COMPLETE set of listed worker groups among the following? (i) Former employees and agency workers; (ii) trainees and volunteers; (iii) board members and shareholders.

options.text: (i) only.
(i) and (ii) only.
(ii) and (iii) only.
(i) and (iii) only.
(i), (ii) and (iii).

questions.explanation: All three sets of groups appear in the deck’s list. Being within a listed group does not remove the other conditions for a protected disclosure.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slide 9; reporting conditions still matter.

questions.stem: A worker considers making an external disclosure to a prescribed person. Which ONE consideration is specifically identified in the deck?

options.text: Every prescribed person has the same remit for every form of wrongdoing.
The recipient’s official title alone determines protection, regardless of the subject reported.
The wrongdoing should fall within the remit of the prescribed person selected.
An external report is necessarily the same as publishing the information on social media.
Using an external channel removes the need for reasonable belief.

questions.explanation: A prescribed person’s remit must match the wrongdoing reported. External reporting is not a route with identical coverage for every recipient.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slides 10–11.

questions.stem: Which ONE statement preserves the deck’s distinction between protected-disclosure status and routes for penalisation redress?

options.text: Every covered group must bring a penalisation complaint through the same WRC route.
Anyone unable to use this WRC route is necessarily excluded from all protected-disclosure protection.
A report becomes protected only after the worker successfully obtains compensation.
An employer’s denial automatically settles whether penalisation followed a disclosure.
Board members and shareholders may seek civil-court redress rather than using this WRC complaint route.

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes covered groups from the forum for redress: it identifies civil-court rather than this WRC complaint route for board members and shareholders.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slides 11–12; no detailed remedy or time limit is inferred.

questions.stem: Which ONE description best reflects the WRC’s functions in the supplied deck?

options.text: It performs the principal leadership role of individual company boards.
It acts only as an appeal body for Labour Court determinations.
It deals only with criminal prosecutions of workplace misconduct.
Its functions include compliance, information, inspection and dispute-resolution services.
It is limited to issuing non-binding advice without any other workplace role.

questions.explanation: The WRC’s role includes information, compliance, inspection and dispute-resolution functions; it is not limited to appeals or criminal prosecution.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slides 2–4.

questions.stem: Which ONE distinction about Labour Court processes is supported by the supplied deck?

options.text: The Labour Court’s principal role is to carry out company inspections on behalf of boards.
An employment-rights appeal permits unrelated new claims to be added to the original case.
Industrial-relations recommendations are non-binding, whereas employment-rights determinations are legally binding.
Every recommendation and determination has the same non-binding status.
Every workplace complaint must begin in the Labour Court rather than the WRC.

questions.explanation: The deck distinguishes non-binding industrial-relations recommendations from binding employment-rights determinations.
questions.source: Corporate Governance, WRC and Protected Disclosures — supplied lecture slides (https://app.notion.com/p/2a7b0bdce90b4575b2b4412087051c8b) — Slides 6–8.

chapters.title: Foundations of Business Ethics
chapters.description: Ethical questions in business, law, judgement and the need for critical reasoning.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes law from ethics?

options.text: Law is enforceable by public institutions; ethics involves reasoned judgement about right conduct.
Law is personal preference; ethics is always criminal.
Law and ethics are identical.
Ethics applies only to private life.

questions.explanation: Law supplies formal rules and sanctions, while ethical evaluation can extend beyond them.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why can technology create new ethical gaps?

options.text: Innovation may create harms before regulation catches up.
Technology makes every action transparent.
Technology prevents conflicts of interest.
New technology is automatically ethical.

questions.explanation: Rapid innovation can outpace lawmakers and expose issues not covered by existing rules.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why does privatisation raise accountability questions?

options.text: Private organisations may deliver essential services while public accountability mechanisms are weaker.
Private firms cannot affect citizens.
Public services have no stakeholders.
Accountability concerns only profit.

questions.explanation: When essential functions move to firms, questions arise about transparency, responsibility and public interest.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What does critical ethical thinking require?

options.text: Examining reasons, evidence, stakeholders and consequences rather than relying on slogans
Choosing the first intuition only
Treating legality as the sole criterion
Ignoring uncertainty

questions.explanation: Ethical judgement should test assumptions and competing reasons.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: What is the most defensible role for evidence in ethical judgement?

options.text: Values make evidence unnecessary.
Ethics begins by assuming allegations are true.
Evidence establishes relevant facts while frameworks evaluate what those facts require.
Facts alone mechanically produce one moral answer.

questions.explanation: Good reasoning separates factual claims from the ethical evaluation built on them.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 1–3 and Readings 1–4

chapters.title: Corporate Purpose & Responsibility
chapters.description: Friedman’s shareholder argument, corporate power and stakeholder consequences.

questions.stem: Which stakeholder is directly affected when a supplier cuts safety standards to meet a buyer’s price target?

options.text: Supply-chain workers
Only the buyer’s shareholders
No one outside the contract
Only tax authorities

questions.explanation: Commercial pressure can transfer risk to workers deeper in the supply chain.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 and Reading 1 notes

questions.stem: What ethical tension is illustrated by very low retail prices linked to poor supply-chain conditions?

options.text: Consumer affordability versus responsibility for production impacts
Law versus mathematics
Technology versus language
Marketing versus accounting only

questions.explanation: Cheap goods can benefit consumers while hiding costs borne by vulnerable workers or communities.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 and Reading 1 notes

questions.stem: What is the strongest reason to examine corporate power ethically?

options.text: Business decisions can shape public choices and distribute risks beyond the firm.
Power guarantees good judgement.
Only governments affect society.
Corporate decisions concern owners alone.

questions.explanation: Scale and influence can create responsibilities beyond ordinary private transactions.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Which response best evaluates a profitable but harmful decision?

options.text: Consider profitability alongside duties, stakeholder harms and alternatives.
Accept it because profit settles every ethical question.
Reject it only if competitors complain.
Ignore people not named in the contract.

questions.explanation: Ethical analysis asks whether profit was achieved through acceptable treatment and consequences.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Which claim avoids oversimplifying the shareholder–stakeholder debate?

options.text: Profit is necessary for business, but its pursuit is constrained by rules and the effects imposed on others.
Profit and ethics can never coexist.
Any social initiative is automatically ethical.
Stakeholders always agree.

questions.explanation: A balanced analysis recognises commercial purpose while evaluating means, external effects and accountability.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 1 notes

questions.stem: Why can mixed motives still produce an ethical action?

options.text: Good intent guarantees good impact.
Motives never matter.
Commercial benefit does not erase genuine stakeholder benefit, though credibility needs evidence.
Any profit makes an action unethical.

questions.explanation: Ethical assessment can consider motives, methods and outcomes together.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 1 and 6; Reading 7

questions.stem: What is purpose-washing?

options.text: Changing a legal structure.
Paying ordinary suppliers.
Promoting a social purpose that is not matched by core operations or accountability.
Publishing audited impact data.

questions.explanation: A purpose claim is weak when practice and incentives contradict it.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 1 and 6; Reading 7

questions.stem: Which question best tests corporate responsibility for a supplier?

options.text: Did the buyer avoid direct employment?
Was the product popular?
What influence, knowledge and foreseeable effects did the buyer have?
Is the supplier in another country?

questions.explanation: Responsibility depends on power, knowledge and effects, not only formal ownership.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 1 and 6; Reading 7

questions.stem: Why can limited liability strengthen the case for social duties?

options.text: Society grants owners protection from some losses, raising reciprocal questions about corporate impacts.
It makes shareholders liable without limit.
It removes corporate legal identity.
It guarantees philanthropy.

questions.explanation: The legal privilege can be paired with expectations of responsible conduct.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 1 and 6; Reading 7

questions.stem: Reading 7 — Reich’s critique of CSR. Which ONE statement most closely reflects his argument?

options.text: Profit incentives can constrain voluntary corporate promises, making enforceable rules and penalties important.
Every profitable social initiative necessarily demonstrates that regulation is unnecessary.
Voluntary promises remove the need for democratic regulation and enforcement.
The existence of a public commitment establishes that a company will bear any cost to fulfil it.
Corporate leaders can always solve social problems without changing the incentives they face.

questions.explanation: Reich argues that voluntary CSR is constrained by profit incentives, which is why enforceable rules and penalties matter in his critique.
questions.source: Reading 7 — Why Corporate Social Responsibility is BS (https://app.notion.com/p/e5786b9b093a43de885dcf504b85cdec)

chapters.title: Authority, Roles & Situational Pressure
chapters.description: Stanford prison and Milgram studies, obedience, roles and situational explanations.

questions.stem: What broad question did the Stanford prison study appear to investigate?

options.text: How assigned social roles and institutional settings influence behaviour
How prices reach equilibrium
How databases store records
How exercise affects memory

questions.explanation: The study examined behaviour in a simulated prison environment.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What later criticism weakens the claim that Stanford guards became cruel spontaneously?

options.text: Guards received orientation and some were encouraged to adopt particular roles.
No participants were assigned roles.
The study used no prison setting.
Every participant refused to continue immediately.

questions.explanation: Coaching and demand characteristics make it harder to attribute behaviour purely to the situation.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What is a demand characteristic?

options.text: A cue that leads participants to behave as they think the study expects
A market shortage
A legal duty to publish results
A personality disorder

questions.explanation: Participants may perform an expected role rather than reveal natural behaviour.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: What lesson can still be drawn cautiously from the Stanford study?

options.text: Authority can frame harmful conduct as serving a legitimate or greater purpose.
Every person becomes sadistic in a uniform.
Situations never influence conduct.
The study proves one universal personality type.

questions.explanation: Even with methodological flaws, role expectations and legitimising narratives can influence conduct.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: In Milgram’s classic setup, what role did participants believe they had?

options.text: Teacher administering shocks for incorrect answers
Prison guard
Corporate auditor
Election observer

questions.explanation: Participants were assigned the teacher role while the learner was part of the experimental setup.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 and Reading 2 notes

questions.stem: What is the agentic state explanation of obedience?

options.text: A person sees themselves as carrying out an authority’s wishes and shifts responsibility upward.
A person becomes financially independent.
A group reaches unanimous agreement.
A participant forgets the instructions.

questions.explanation: Perceived agency and responsibility move toward the authority figure.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Which change tended to reduce obedience in Milgram-style variations?

options.text: Peers openly resisting the authority
Increasing the authority’s proximity
Increasing institutional prestige
Making escalation gradual

questions.explanation: Social support for resistance makes disobedience more psychologically available.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Why can gradual escalation increase compliance?

options.text: Each small step makes the next step easier to rationalise and creates commitment.
It makes the authority disappear.
It removes every consequence.
It turns orders into laws.

questions.explanation: Incremental increases can bind a person to previous choices before the full severity is apparent.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 notes

questions.stem: Which is a valid ethical criticism of Milgram’s study?

options.text: Participants experienced deception and significant distress, raising consent and withdrawal concerns.
The study had no human participants.
It revealed participants’ real names publicly in class.
It measured only market prices.

questions.explanation: The design placed participants under pressure while concealing the study’s true purpose.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 and Reading 2 notes

questions.stem: In Milgram’s study, what did the learner’s protests test?

options.text: Whether memory improves with real shocks.
Whether teachers knew the learner personally.
Whether the machine measured intelligence.
Whether participants would continue under authority despite apparent harm.

questions.explanation: The conflict between obedience and concern for the learner was central.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 and Reading 2

questions.stem: Why does experimenter distance tend to reduce obedience?

options.text: The authority becomes less immediate and easier to resist.
The learner becomes invisible.
The shocks become real.
Peers become more obedient automatically.

questions.explanation: Proximity affects the authority’s social pressure.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 and Reading 2

questions.stem: Why is “I was following orders” not a complete moral defence?

options.text: Authorities always possess better ethics.
Responsibility belongs only to victims.
Situational pressure helps explain conduct but does not automatically remove agency or responsibility.
Orders make every act lawful.

questions.explanation: Explanation and excuse are separate questions.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 and Reading 2

questions.stem: What is the safest conclusion from the Stanford prison evidence?

options.text: The study had no demand characteristics.
Role expectations and researcher cues can influence behaviour, but the classic spontaneous-sadism claim is overstated.
Any assigned guard becomes cruel.
The study proves personality never matters.

questions.explanation: Coaching and performance weaken the strongest original claim.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 and Reading 2

questions.stem: Why are later obedience studies not directly percentage-comparable with Milgram’s classic condition?

options.text: Methods, safeguards, samples and stopping rules differ.
Percentages cannot describe behaviour.
Modern participants never face authority.
Milgram used no experimental design.

questions.explanation: Design differences limit simple numerical comparison.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 2 and Reading 2

questions.stem: Reading 2 — Milgram. Which ONE statement about the classic condition described in the reading is TRUE?

options.text: Every participant stopped as soon as the learner first objected.
The results were unaffected by changes to the experimental situation.
About 65% continued to the maximum labelled 450 volts, although the shocks were not real.
The study compared only people already known to have violent criminal records.
About 65% knowingly administered real 450-volt shocks to another participant.

questions.explanation: The reading describes about 65% reaching the maximum labelled voltage in the classic condition. The learner was not receiving real shocks.
questions.source: Reading 2 — The Milgram Shock Experiment (https://app.notion.com/p/337a2d3d812648469e04f61314c8c348)

chapters.title: Bias, Rationalisation & Leadership
chapters.description: Cognitive biases and psychological mechanisms that shape ethical judgement.

questions.stem: How does an amoral manager differ from an immoral manager?

options.text: An amoral manager shows little concern for moral considerations; an immoral manager knowingly acts against them.
They are identical by definition.
An amoral manager always follows every duty.
An immoral manager is unaware of consequences.

questions.explanation: The distinction concerns indifference to ethics versus conscious wrongdoing.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: A board interprets ambiguous evidence as confirming its existing strategy. Which bias fits best?

options.text: Limited liability
Act utilitarianism
Externality
Biased assimilation

questions.explanation: Prior commitments shape how mixed evidence is evaluated.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3

questions.stem: What is the best organisational response to overconfidence?

options.text: Reward certainty and suppress dissent.
Remove all data.
Let the most senior view prevail.
Independent challenge, decision records and tests against disconfirming evidence.

questions.explanation: Structured challenge reduces reliance on confidence as evidence.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3

chapters.title: Ethical Culture, Incentives & Organisational Systems
chapters.description: How language, incentives, distance, governance and leadership shape conduct.

questions.stem: How can reward systems undermine ethical conduct?

options.text: They can make short-term targets more salient than duties or stakeholder harm.
Rewards eliminate self-interest.
Bonuses automatically improve oversight.
Targets cannot influence behaviour.

questions.explanation: People respond to what the organisation measures and rewards.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 notes

questions.stem: Which control best addresses pressure to manipulate sales figures?

options.text: Combine realistic targets with independent checks, speak-up channels and consequences for misreporting.
Raise targets and remove audits.
Reward results regardless of method.
Keep reporting rules ambiguous.

questions.explanation: Aligned incentives and oversight reduce both pressure and opportunity for misconduct.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 notes

questions.stem: Why is an ethics code alone often insufficient?

options.text: Actual incentives, leadership behaviour and enforcement may contradict the document.
Written rules cannot be read.
Codes are always illegal.
Employees never notice leaders.

questions.explanation: Culture is produced by practice and accountability, not merely formal statements.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 1–3 notes

questions.stem: What is “tone at the top”?

options.text: The example and priorities communicated by senior leaders
The volume of a manager’s voice
A public advertising slogan only
A legal definition of profit

questions.explanation: Employees infer acceptable conduct from what leaders do, reward and tolerate.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 notes

questions.stem: Which organisational feature helps counter conformity?

options.text: Protected channels for challenge and leaders who invite dissent
Punishing all disagreement
Keeping decisions secret
Rewarding only unanimity

questions.explanation: Psychological safety and protected escalation make concerns easier to raise.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 notes

questions.stem: What makes an ethical programme credible?

options.text: Consistent leadership, aligned incentives, training, reporting routes, investigation and accountability
A slogan with no operational change
A single annual email
Profit growth alone

questions.explanation: Credibility requires systems that reinforce stated values in everyday decisions.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 1–3 and Reading 4 notes

questions.stem: What does psychological safety support?

options.text: Secrecy around failures.
Removal of accountability.
Raising concerns and admitting mistakes without disproportionate retaliation.
Guaranteed agreement with leaders.

questions.explanation: People are more likely to surface risk when challenge is safe.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 and Reading 4

questions.stem: Why should an ethics hotline be independent and protected?

options.text: Anonymous concerns are always true.
Employees may otherwise fear retaliation or suppression by implicated managers.
Independence removes the need to investigate.
Only customers can report concerns.

questions.explanation: Protected channels improve access while allegations still require fair investigation.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 and Reading 4

questions.stem: What is incentive compatibility in an ethics programme?

options.text: Targets and rewards support rather than undermine stated standards.
Every employee receives the same pay.
Rules are hidden from staff.
Profit is never measured.

questions.explanation: Conduct follows what organisations reward as well as what they say.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 and Reading 4

questions.stem: Which metric best tests whether an ethics programme works?

options.text: The chief executive’s speech count.
Patterns in reporting, investigation, retaliation, outcomes and repeated misconduct.
The number of posters printed.
The length of the code alone.

questions.explanation: Operational evidence is more informative than symbolic activity.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 and Reading 4

questions.stem: What is diffusion of responsibility?

options.text: One leader accepts every consequence.
A firm discloses its supply chain.
A whistleblower documents a concern.
Accountability weakens because each participant assumes someone else owns the issue.

questions.explanation: Fragmented roles can allow foreseeable harms to fall between functions.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 and Reading 4

chapters.title: Externalities, Global Business & Evidence
chapters.description: Stakeholder impacts, externalised costs, global supply chains and evidence-based ethical claims.

questions.stem: What is a negative externality?

options.text: A cost imposed on people outside the market transaction
A discount received by a buyer
A cost recorded fully in the seller’s accounts
A voluntary donation

questions.explanation: Externalities occur when some consequences fall on third parties and are omitted from the private exchange.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why are externalities ethically important?

options.text: People may bear harms without choosing or benefiting from the transaction.
They always increase profit.
They affect only accountants.
They are included automatically in every price.

questions.explanation: Consent, fairness and responsibility become concerns when costs are shifted to outsiders.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: Why should claims about fast-fashion harm be made carefully?

options.text: Specific allegations require reliable evidence rather than assumption or viral repetition.
Fast fashion has no ethical issues.
Evidence is irrelevant to ethics.
Only prices may be discussed.

questions.explanation: Ethical criticism is stronger when it distinguishes documented facts from general suspicion.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: How can a company externalise environmental costs?

options.text: By leaving pollution or resource depletion for communities and future generations to bear
By paying all clean-up costs itself
By reducing harmful emissions
By disclosing verified impacts

questions.explanation: Externalisation shifts costs away from the firm and transaction.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What did the facial-scar perception example illustrate?

options.text: Expectations can shape how people interpret ambiguous social treatment.
Visible scars determine every interaction.
Perception always matches objective treatment.
Experiments cannot use deception.

questions.explanation: Participants’ expectations influenced their interpretation even when the apparent scar had been removed.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 notes

questions.stem: What is the best method for evaluating a dramatic corporate-ethics claim?

options.text: Identify the claim, check credible evidence, consider alternative explanations and separate fact from inference.
Share it immediately if it confirms prior beliefs.
Assume legality proves morality.
Ignore who is affected.

questions.explanation: Evidence-based ethical analysis guards against biased assimilation and unsupported accusation.
questions.source: MG2008 Lectures 2–3 and Reading 4 notes

questions.stem: A product’s low price excludes pollution costs borne by residents. What is this?

options.text: Consumer surplus only
A positive right
A sunk cost
A negative externality

questions.explanation: Part of the social cost is shifted outside the transaction.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 and Readings 3–4

questions.stem: Why is a vivid photograph insufficient proof of a general business claim?

options.text: Images cannot contain information.
Only numerical evidence is ethical.
One example proves every case.
It may illustrate harm without establishing prevalence, causation or representativeness.

questions.explanation: Evidence quality depends on how well it supports the scope of the claim.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 and Readings 3–4

questions.stem: What does due diligence require in a high-risk supply chain?

options.text: Assume distance removes responsibility.
Identify, prevent, mitigate and account for foreseeable harms.
Rely solely on a supplier promise.
Stop collecting evidence.

questions.explanation: Due diligence is an ongoing risk-management and accountability process.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 and Readings 3–4

questions.stem: Why may consumers struggle to discipline harmful supply chains?

options.text: Consumers have perfect traceability.
Every ethical product is cheaper.
Firms cannot change suppliers.
Information is incomplete and individual purchasing power is limited.

questions.explanation: Information and collective-action problems constrain consumer choice.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 and Readings 3–4

questions.stem: Which statement best avoids an ethical overclaim?

options.text: The evidence indicates a risk requiring investigation, but does not yet prove every actor caused the harm.
The allegation proves guilt.
No documented harm can ever occur.
Profit establishes innocence.

questions.explanation: Calibrated claims preserve uncertainty while taking credible risks seriously.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 3 and Readings 3–4

questions.stem: A firm publishes an ambitious social-purpose campaign while its working practices contradict the message. Which ONE question should an ethical assessment prioritise?

options.text: Whether any social-purpose message must be rejected regardless of what the firm actually does.
Whether the campaign is popular enough to make operational evidence unnecessary.
Whether the campaign’s production budget establishes the sincerity of the commitment.
Whether the public commitment is supported by substantive changes in corporate conduct.
Whether publicity alone is an adequate substitute for examining affected workers’ circumstances.

questions.explanation: A social-purpose message should be checked against substantive operations. Publicity, popularity and expenditure alone do not establish responsible conduct.
questions.source: Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8135a529c4c28c26f9c1); Reading 3 — Woke-washing and culture-war branding (https://app.notion.com/p/9977157cec62436aadf1b64f409d9452)

questions.stem: Reading 3 — Woke-washing. Which ONE approach is most consistent with the critique?

options.text: Assess only whether the slogan attracts attention, rather than what the firm does.
Treat criticism of a campaign as proof that its stated social goal is undesirable.
Treat a progressive campaign as sufficient proof that the firm’s operations are ethical.
Compare a firm’s social-purpose message with its labour, supply-chain and other substantive practices.
Assume that every social-purpose campaign is insincere without examining evidence.

questions.explanation: The woke-washing critique tests whether stated social commitments match operations; neither accepting slogans nor rejecting every campaign without evidence is sufficient.
questions.source: Reading 3 — Woke-washing and culture-war branding (https://app.notion.com/p/9977157cec62436aadf1b64f409d9452)

chapters.title: Consequences, Context & Utilitarianism
chapters.description: Consequentialism, relativism, Bentham, Mill and cost–benefit reasoning.

questions.stem: What does moral relativism claim?

options.text: Law and ethics are identical.
Standards are shaped by cultural context.
One objective rule is obvious everywhere.
Consequences never matter.

questions.explanation: Relativism emphasises the cultural formation of moral judgement.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 4; Reading 5

questions.stem: A safety measure costs €1 million and prevents widespread serious harm. What must utilitarian analysis include?

options.text: All significant stakeholder benefits and costs, not profit alone.
Only the firm’s cash outlay.
Only majority preferences.
Only legal penalties.

questions.explanation: Welfare analysis counts external and long-term consequences.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 4; Reading 5

questions.stem: In the trolley problem, what feature creates the classic utilitarian appeal?

options.text: Duties are legally defined.
The outcome is unknowable by design.
Sacrificing one appears to save a larger number.
No one is harmed.

questions.explanation: The case tests whether aggregate welfare justifies imposing a severe cost on one.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 4; Reading 5

chapters.title: Duties, Character, Rights & Justice
chapters.description: Kant, virtue ethics, rights, Rawls, discourse ethics and pluralism.

questions.stem: How does Rawls differ from utilitarianism?

options.text: Rawls ignores fairness.
Rawls treats profit as the only good.
There is no difference.
Rawls protects basic liberties and the least advantaged rather than simply maximising the total.

questions.explanation: Justice as fairness constrains aggregate maximisation.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 5; Reading 6

questions.stem: What does ethical pluralism recommend?

options.text: Treat every answer as equally valid.
Abandon principles.
Choose the most profitable theory.
Use multiple relevant frameworks and seek justified overlap rather than one automatic test.

questions.explanation: Different frameworks expose different moral features of a dilemma.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 5; Reading 6

chapters.title: Stakeholders, Governance & CSR
chapters.description: Stakeholder classifications, corporate governance and CSR credibility.

questions.stem: Who is a stakeholder?

options.text: Only an owner of shares.
Only a government regulator.
Only a paying customer.
A person or group that affects or is affected by the organisation.

questions.explanation: Stakeholding is broader than equity ownership.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6; Readings 7 and 9

questions.stem: Why should Dodge v Ford be read cautiously?

options.text: It concerns no corporation.
It prohibits managerial judgement.
A historical case does not prove a universal duty to maximise short-term profit at any cost.
It abolished shareholder interests.

questions.explanation: Later doctrine and context complicate the simplified shareholder-primacy slogan.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6; Readings 7 and 9

questions.stem: What is credible CSR most likely to show?

options.text: Governance, resources and measurable operational change aligned with the claim.
A donation unrelated to core harm.
A campaign with no targets.
Legal compliance presented as exceptional generosity.

questions.explanation: Credibility depends on what the business changes and can account for.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6; Readings 7 and 9

questions.stem: Why can philanthropy fail to offset harmful core operations?

options.text: Philanthropy is always illegal.
The scale and source of harm may outweigh a separate charitable benefit.
Donations erase causation.
Stakeholders consider only intent.

questions.explanation: CSR must be assessed against the whole business model.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 6; Readings 7 and 9

questions.stem: Which ONE sequence correctly gives the four responsibilities in Carroll’s CSR pyramid, from its base upwards?

options.text: Philanthropic, ethical, legal, economic.
Economic, legal, ethical, philanthropic.
Legal, economic, philanthropic, ethical.
Economic, philanthropic, legal, ethical.
Ethical, legal, economic, philanthropic.

questions.explanation: Carroll’s pyramid places economic responsibilities at the base, followed by legal, ethical and philanthropic responsibilities.
questions.source: Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8135a529c4c28c26f9c1)

chapters.title: Consumerism, GDP & Wellbeing
chapters.description: Consumer identity, GDP limits, wellbeing measures and degrowth.

questions.stem: What is consumerism in the lecture?

options.text: Any act of buying necessities.
A ban on advertising.
A national accounting measure.
A pattern linking identity and wellbeing strongly to acquiring goods and services.

questions.explanation: Consumerism concerns social meaning and continual acquisition, not purchase alone.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 7; Readings 8, 10 and 11

questions.stem: What benefit of GDP growth should a balanced critique retain?

options.text: Growth never affects life expectancy.
Only symbolic consumption changes.
GDP automatically ensures equality.
Growth has supported major improvements in material living standards and health.

questions.explanation: GDP is useful even though it is not sufficient.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 7; Readings 8, 10 and 11

questions.stem: What is symbolic consumption?

options.text: Reducing product variety.
Buying partly to express identity, status or belonging.
Purchasing only basic food.
Measuring public output.

questions.explanation: Products can carry social meaning beyond practical function.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 7; Readings 8, 10 and 11

questions.stem: What are the three elements of the triple bottom line?

options.text: People, planet and profit.
Price, promotion and place.
Law, ethics and morals.
Income, inflation and interest.

questions.explanation: The framework broadens performance beyond finance.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 7; Readings 8, 10 and 11

questions.stem: What does Gross National Happiness challenge?

options.text: The assumption that GDP growth alone represents national progress.
The value of social support.
The use of public policy.
The existence of environmental limits.

questions.explanation: It treats happiness, equity and sustainability as policy goals.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 7; Readings 8, 10 and 11

questions.stem: Which is one of Pretty et al.’s wellbeing pathways?

options.text: Longer commuting time.
Family and community connections.
Maximum advertising exposure.
Higher product turnover.

questions.explanation: Social connection is one of six pathways alongside food, activity, mind, nature and meaningful possessions.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 7; Readings 8, 10 and 11

questions.stem: Why can apparent brand variety be misleading?

options.text: Every brand is legally independent.
Ownership never affects choice.
Labels disclose all supply chains.
Many brands may share common owners and concentrated decision power.

questions.explanation: Market concentration can reduce meaningful diversity behind the shelf.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 7; Readings 8, 10 and 11

questions.stem: What ethical issue do warning labels raise?

options.text: Whether information is always manipulation.
Whether health has no social cost.
Whether consumers lack all agency.
How to support informed autonomy without ignoring industry design and vulnerable consumers.

It records only non-market activities such as unpaid care.
It does not by itself capture health, relationships, environmental conditions and the quality of everyday life.
A rise in output establishes that all six wellbeing pathways have improved.
An unchanged GDP figure establishes that nobody’s wellbeing can improve.

options.text: A requirement that low-income households give up access to basic goods.
A policy limited to reducing all household purchases by the same percentage.
A temporary fall in GDP with no change to institutions or social priorities.
A broader reorganisation of social priorities and ways of living, rather than simply asking everyone to buy less.
A strategy for increasing consumption indefinitely by changing product labels.

chapters.title: Bottom of the Pyramid, Fairtrade & Microfinance
chapters.description: Low-income markets, appropriate innovation, trade, aid and finance.

questions.stem: Who are the Bottom of the Pyramid in this context?

options.text: Government employees.
Corporate shareholders.
Large populations living on very low incomes and often underserved by mainstream business.
Only wealthy early adopters.

questions.explanation: BOP refers to low-income consumers and producers excluded from conventional markets.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 8; Readings 12–16

questions.stem: What is the poverty penalty?

options.text: A reward for saving.
A subsidy to large firms.
Poor consumers may pay more per unit or face worse terms because of limited access and scale.
A tax charged only on profit.

questions.explanation: Small purchases, weak infrastructure and lack of credit can raise effective costs.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 8; Readings 12–16

questions.stem: What does co-creation add to BOP design?

options.text: Removal of customer feedback.
Guaranteed profit.
Local knowledge and participation in defining useful solutions.
A foreign design imposed unchanged.

questions.explanation: Local participation reduces the risk of unsuitable products.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 8; Readings 12–16

questions.stem: What is Project Shakti?

options.text: A tobacco settlement.
A climate treaty.
A social-media algorithm.
A model training and financing rural women to distribute products in India.

questions.explanation: It combines livelihood opportunities with hard-to-reach distribution.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 8; Readings 12–16

questions.stem: What is a central ethical question about microfinance?

options.text: Whether repayment is always harmful.
Whether access to credit creates durable empowerment or burdens vulnerable borrowers with debt.
Whether loans contain any numbers.
Whether banks can use money.

questions.explanation: Repayment rates alone do not establish positive welfare impact.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 8; Readings 12–16

questions.stem: What is cultural pollution in BOP debates?

options.text: Marketing and products may displace local practices and impose outside aspirations.
A measurable air pollutant only.
Any cultural exchange.
Local product design.

questions.explanation: Commercial influence can alter values and practices as well as consumption.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 8; Readings 12–16

questions.stem: Why should microfinance evaluation look beyond repayment?

options.text: Positive impact requires default.
Borrowers may repay through hardship, refinancing or sacrifice without improved wellbeing.
Repayment data are never real.
Only lenders are stakeholders.

questions.explanation: Financial performance is not identical to social outcome.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 8; Readings 12–16

questions.stem: A detergent sachet costs little to buy today but more per gram than a large pack. Which ONE statement is TRUE?

A low purchase price eliminates the need to consider packaging waste.
Affordability today and long-run unit cost are the same measure.
A higher unit price establishes that access has not changed at all.
Lower upfront cost can improve access without producing the lowest unit price.

questions.explanation: A small package can be accessible within today’s budget while costing more per gram. Upfront affordability and unit value are different measures.

questions.stem: Reading 12 — TOMS. Which ONE distinction is central to the critique of giving shoes through a purchase-linked donation model?

options.text: The number of shoes delivered by itself measures every relevant educational and welfare outcome.
An in-kind donation necessarily produces no benefit for any recipient.
A donor’s positive feeling and good intention do not establish that the intervention best addresses recipients’ needs.
A purchase-linked donation proves that structural poverty has been removed.
Recipients’ own circumstances are irrelevant once a donation is free.

questions.explanation: The TOMS critique distinguishes donor satisfaction and outputs from evidence of benefit in recipients’ circumstances. Good intentions do not settle effectiveness.

questions.stem: Reading 15 — Rugasira. Which ONE proposal most closely reflects his critique of relying on Fairtrade alone?

options.text: Replace all producer enterprise with dependence on charitable purchases.
Treat a consumer’s compassionate intention as sufficient evidence of development.
Assume that removing tariffs automatically removes every non-tariff barrier.
Enable producers to add value locally and obtain meaningful market access, rather than relying only on small premiums.
Concentrate all processing abroad because the location of value addition is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Rugasira emphasises value addition and meaningful market access, rather than assuming that premiums alone provide durable development.
