chapters.title: Tobacco, Pharma & OxyContin
chapters.description: Addiction, information asymmetry, marketing and distributed accountability.

questions.stem: Why does addiction complicate the consumer-choice defence?

options.text: Consumers lose every form of agency.
Repeated purchase may not reflect fully free and informed choice.
Addiction increases information symmetry.
Harm becomes irrelevant when a product is legal.

questions.explanation: Dependence can weaken autonomy without removing all personal responsibility.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: What is information asymmetry in the tobacco or opioid cases?

options.text: Only regulators know product prices.
Advertising removes uncertainty.
Firms may know more about risks than consumers, patients or prescribers.
Everyone has identical evidence.

questions.explanation: Unequal knowledge can undermine informed consent.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: Why are price discounts a form of tobacco promotion?

options.text: They eliminate segmentation.
They lower effective prices and can encourage purchase even without a conventional advert.
They increase every health warning.
They prohibit retailer sales.

questions.explanation: Marketing includes pricing and distribution incentives.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: What ethical problem arises from targeting communities already facing disadvantage?

options.text: Marketing may exploit vulnerability and concentrate harm.
Segmentation is always neutral.
Only shareholders are affected.
Legal products have no externalities.

questions.explanation: Unequal exposure matters to justice and stakeholder analysis.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: What is a public-health externality of addictive products?

options.text: Treatment and family costs fall partly on people outside the sale.
The buyer pays a listed price.
The firm records revenue.
A shareholder receives a dividend.

questions.explanation: Private transactions can transfer costs to health systems and communities.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: Why does the OxyContin case broaden responsibility beyond Purdue?

options.text: Only the final consumer acts.
Legal settlements remove causation.
Supply chains cannot share responsibility.
Consultants, distributors, prescribers and regulators may contribute to cumulative harm.

questions.explanation: Complex harm can arise from interacting decisions across a system.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: What governance failure can aggressive sales incentives create?

options.text: Employees may minimise risk information to meet targets.
Targets guarantee accurate disclosure.
Bonuses eliminate conflicts of interest.
Sales teams set public-health law.

questions.explanation: Incentives can reward volume while weakening risk control.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: Does a settlement alone establish moral accountability?

options.text: Yes; money proves sincere remorse.
Yes; courts decide every ethical question.
No; settlements are never relevant.
No; payment can resolve claims while responsibility is still denied or contested.

questions.explanation: Legal resolution and moral acknowledgement are related but distinct.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: How would Kantian ethics assess deceptive risk marketing?

options.text: It asks only whether competitors do it.
It uses patients as means by undermining informed agency.
It is acceptable whenever profitable.
It counts only aggregate pleasure.

questions.explanation: Respect for persons requires truthful information and non-manipulation.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

questions.stem: What is the strongest utilitarian test of an addictive product strategy?

options.text: Count company revenue only.
Assume every purchase adds welfare.
Ignore indirect consequences.
Compare total benefits with health, family and social harms over time.

questions.explanation: Utilitarianism requires the full balance of stakeholder outcomes.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 9

chapters.title: Ultra-Processed Food & Market Power
chapters.description: Food formulation, evidence, concentration, autonomy and responsibility.

questions.stem: What distinguishes ultra-processed food from ordinary processed food?

options.text: Any cooked food is ultra-processed.
Processing means adding water only.
UPFs contain one recognisable ingredient.
UPFs are industrial formulations using multiple ingredients and processes for convenience, shelf life and palatability.

questions.explanation: The category concerns formulation and industrial processing, not any alteration.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: Why does an association between UPF intake and disease not by itself prove causation?

options.text: Health outcomes cannot be measured.
Other factors and study design may explain part of the relationship.
Associations contain no evidence.
Causation requires a company admission.

questions.explanation: Observational evidence needs careful interpretation and corroboration.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: What is the cautious conclusion from food–drug reward similarities?

options.text: Reward mechanisms may overlap, but similarity does not prove identical addiction.
Sugar and cocaine are ethically identical.
Food has no reward effect.
Every consumer becomes dependent.

questions.explanation: Analogy can guide questions without settling degree or causality.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: How can market concentration reduce meaningful consumer choice?

options.text: Retailers cannot influence choice.
A few firms may control formulation, prices, distribution and shelf access.
More brands always mean more owners.
Concentration removes bargaining power from large firms.

questions.explanation: Visible variety may mask concentrated control.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: Why are farmers stakeholders in food-market concentration?

options.text: Farmers buy no food.
Only consumers face bargaining power.
Concentration guarantees higher farm income.
Dominant buyers can shape terms, prices and market access.

questions.explanation: Power can be exercised upstream as well as toward consumers.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: What autonomy concern arises from engineered palatability?

options.text: Design may exploit predictable cues to increase consumption beyond reflective choice.
Taste eliminates all responsibility.
Pleasure is always unethical.
Formulation cannot influence behaviour.

questions.explanation: The concern is intentional use of superior behavioural knowledge.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: How can GLP-1 medicines create a food–pharma incentive conflict?

options.text: Treatment and prevention always align.
One sector may profit from treating conditions partly linked to another sector’s products.
Medicines remove every prevention need.
Food firms sell no health-related products.

questions.explanation: Commercial systems may reward treatment without correcting causes.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: Why is reformulation not necessarily business-model change?

options.text: Reformulation removes market power.
Health labels prevent overconsumption.
A healthier product can coexist with aggressive volume growth and marketing.
Any ingredient change ends externalities.

questions.explanation: Impact depends on total operations and consumption, not one product metric.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: What evidence would strengthen a causal UPF claim?

options.text: A single dramatic headline.
One brand advertisement.
A correlation with no controls.
Converging results from appropriate longitudinal, experimental and mechanistic research.

questions.explanation: Multiple methods can address confounding and mechanisms.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

questions.stem: What is shared responsibility in this context?

options.text: Only consumers matter.
Only manufacturers matter.
Responsibility must be equal among all actors.
Consumers retain agency while firms, retailers and regulators also shape choices and risks.

questions.explanation: Responsibility can be distributed unequally according to power and knowledge.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 10; Reading 20

chapters.title: AI, Social Media & Data Ethics
chapters.description: AI reliability, concentration, labour, profiling and platform responsibility.

questions.stem: What is an AI hallucination?

options.text: A legal ownership form.
A guaranteed prediction.
A confident output that is unsupported or false.
A verified training record.

questions.explanation: Generative systems can produce plausible language without factual grounding.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: Why are hallucinations especially concerning in high-stakes use?

options.text: Errors become harmless at scale.
Confidence proves accuracy.
Users may rely on false outputs in decisions affecting rights, safety or health.
High-stakes users need no evidence.

questions.explanation: Consequences magnify the need for validation and oversight.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: What economic risk can AI investment concentration create?

options.text: Valuation proves social benefit.
Technology firms cannot fail.
A reversal in expectations can affect markets and exposed economies.
Concentration guarantees stable returns.

questions.explanation: Systemic exposure matters beyond model behaviour.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: What labour tension accompanies AI productivity claims?

options.text: Productivity and labour are unrelated.
Only investors are stakeholders.
Gains may depend partly on replacing work, affecting employment and income distribution.
Automation always raises every wage.

questions.explanation: Efficiency benefits can be distributed unevenly.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: When can personalisation become manipulation?

options.text: Only when users pay money.
When a recommendation is accurate.
When hidden profiling exploits vulnerabilities to steer choices against informed interests.
Whenever content is relevant.

questions.explanation: Transparency, autonomy and power distinguish assistance from exploitation.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: Why can a platform bear responsibility for user-generated content?

options.text: Hosting removes all causal influence.
Algorithms are neutral by definition.
Users cannot be stakeholders.
Its ranking and recommendation systems shape reach, incentives and foreseeable harm.

questions.explanation: Design choices mediate what receives attention.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: What is an addictive-design conflict of interest?

options.text: Design cannot affect habits.
Revenue rises with engagement even when compulsive use harms users.
Users and platforms always want identical outcomes.
Attention has no commercial value.

questions.explanation: The business model can reward behaviour contrary to wellbeing.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: Why are children treated as especially vulnerable online?

options.text: Advertising cannot reach minors.
Their judgement and resistance to persuasive design are still developing.
Children never use platforms.
Age has no relationship to consent.

questions.explanation: Developmental vulnerability can justify stronger duties and safeguards.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: Which governance response best fits high-risk AI deployment?

options.text: Hide known limitations.
Independent evaluation, monitoring, human accountability and limits proportionate to harm.
Rely on the developer’s confidence only.
Deploy everywhere before testing.

questions.explanation: Risk governance needs evidence, control and clear responsibility.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 11; Reading 22

questions.stem: Reading 22 — Cambridge Analytica. Which ONE sequence best describes the predictive process explained in the article?

options.text: Use questionnaire and like data to train predictions about traits, then use inferred profiles to support targeted messaging.
Replace statistical inference with a complete questionnaire administered to every person targeted.
Infer each individual’s vote with certainty from a single like, without a training process.
Collect no personal data and assign personality traits purely at random.
Prove that every person receiving an advertisement changed their vote because of it.

questions.explanation: The article explains statistical inference from training data and targeting based on inferred traits; it does not establish certainty about each individual vote or advert effect.

chapters.title: Sustainability, Plastics & Corporate Credibility
chapters.description: Climate justice, circularity, SDGs, plastics and B Corps.

questions.stem: What is environmental justice?

options.text: Treating climate effects as identical everywhere.
Counting emissions without people.
Fair distribution of environmental benefits, harms and decision power.
Maximising recycling labels.

questions.explanation: Communities contributing least may bear the greatest consequences.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: What does a circular economy aim to do?

options.text: Increase disposal after one use.
Rely only on landfill taxes.
Maximise virgin-material extraction.
Design out waste and keep products and materials in use.

questions.explanation: Circular design prioritises prevention, durability, reuse and recovery.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: Why is prevention generally preferred to recycling alone?

options.text: Avoiding waste and virgin production addresses impacts before disposal.
Recycling always uses no energy.
Every recyclable item is recycled.
Prevention eliminates product use.

questions.explanation: End-of-pipe recycling cannot fully offset growing material throughput.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: Why can “recyclable” be a misleading comfort?

options.text: Recyclable products are never collected.
The label proves circularity.
Recycling has no infrastructure needs.
Technical recyclability does not mean collection and actual recycling occur.

questions.explanation: Real outcomes depend on systems, economics and behaviour.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: What greenwashing risk appears in a clean-up alliance formed by major plastic producers?

options.text: Clean-up always changes the core model.
Alliance membership proves impact.
Production volume is irrelevant.
Visible removal may be tiny compared with continued growth in virgin plastic output.

questions.explanation: Credibility requires comparing the initiative with the scale of core operations.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: What is procedural climate justice?

options.text: The richest actor decides alone.
Only total emissions matter.
Lobbying power is ethically neutral.
Affected and vulnerable groups have meaningful influence over decisions.

questions.explanation: Fair process concerns who participates and whose interests shape agreements.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: How should the SDGs be understood for this module?

options.text: A climate treaty limited to emissions.
An interconnected framework for social, economic and environmental progress.
A requirement to memorise every target only.
A corporate certification.

questions.explanation: The lecture emphasises concepts and connections.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: How does a benefit corporation differ from B Corp certification?

options.text: It requires no stakeholder purpose.
It is a legal corporate form available in some jurisdictions.
It is the same B Lab award.
It means tax-exempt charity.

questions.explanation: Legal status and private certification can overlap but are distinct.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: What would best demonstrate credible sustainability strategy?

options.text: Counting only waste collected.
Lifecycle targets, governance, investment and verified reductions aligned with core production.
A slogan without baseline data.
One sponsored event.

questions.explanation: Credibility requires measurable change across the business model.
questions.source: MG2008 Lecture 12; Reading 19

questions.stem: Which ONE statement about independent corporate certification is the most defensible interpretation of the B Corp discussion?

options.text: Independent assessment differs from a company merely making its own claims, but does not remove the need to scrutinise particular conduct.
Certification means that the company cannot pursue a commercial return.
A certified company no longer needs to disclose its supply-chain practices.
A company’s own description of its values is identical to independent certification.
Certification establishes that every product and business decision is ethically beyond criticism.

questions.explanation: Independent certification differs from self-assertion, but it does not establish ethical perfection or remove scrutiny of particular products and practices.

chapters.title: Discussion Group 1: Low-Cost Clothing

questions.stem: Why is that risk not a justification for the status quo?

options.text: Local norms settle ethics.
Low prices prove consent.
Limited alternatives should not excuse unsafe work, lost education or bribery.
Poverty eliminates rights.

questions.explanation: Context shapes remedies but does not erase minimum protections.

Corruption benefits every stakeholder.
Even the claim of legal compliance is doubtful.
The supplier exceeds governance standards.

options.text: How many garments sell?
Would the sourcing rules be accepted without knowing whether one is child, parent, buyer or shareholder?
Which option maximises buyer promotion?
What local practice is most common?

questions.explanation: The veil of ignorance tests impartial fairness.

Ignore household income.
Move quietly to an equally risky supplier.
Accept certification without verification.

The buyer has no agency.
Those bearing the greatest risk often have the least power over price and contracts.

Local voices have no relevance.
Dialogue replaces evidence.

questions.stem: In the clothing-sourcing case, which ONE combination most clearly captures the buyer’s conflict?

Only the supplier’s ability to meet the retailer’s target price.
Whether the buyer’s personal intention is good, regardless of outcomes.
Only the buyer’s prospects of obtaining promotion.

Whether the buyer can avoid being blamed by referring to the agent’s certificate.

(i) and (iii) only.
(ii) only.
(i), (ii) and (iii).
(ii) and (iii) only.

questions.explanation: Safety, education and livelihoods all appear in the case. A response that ignores any one of them leaves a material part of the dilemma unexamined.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group One — Case-study One (https://app.notion.com/p/1c3b411b8c334376a9303b8b90217325)

chapters.title: Discussion Group 2: Casas Bahia
chapters.description: Credit inclusion, behavioural marketing and vulnerable-consumer protection.

questions.stem: What historical monthly interest figure is reported in the case?

options.text: About 4.13%.
About 0.04%.
About 41.3%.
Exactly 8.5%.

questions.explanation: The case reports an average monthly rate of roughly 4.13%.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 2

questions.stem: What historical default rate is reported?

options.text: About 4.13%.
About 30%.
Zero.
About 8.5%.

questions.explanation: The case gives an average default rate of 8.5%.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 2

questions.stem: How can customer data both help and harm?

options.text: Personalisation always benefits customers.
Privacy applies only to governments.
It can improve tailored credit while enabling manipulation and intrusive profiling.
Data have no ethical effects.

questions.explanation: The same capability can support inclusion or exploitation.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 2

questions.stem: What is the inclusion argument for Casas Bahia?

options.text: It charged no interest.
It avoided behavioural marketing.
It gave excluded consumers access to useful goods and credit histories.
It eliminated all poverty.

questions.explanation: The model opened formal access where banks often did not.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 2

questions.stem: What is the exploitation argument?

options.text: Low-income consumers lack all agency.
Credit cannot create utility.
Affordable-looking instalments and emotional selling may obscure high total cost.
Branded goods are always harmful.

questions.explanation: Vulnerability and information gaps can make consent less informed.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 2

questions.stem: Can the model be both empowering and exploitative?

options.text: No; profit proves exploitation only.
Yes; because ethics is purely relative.
Yes; access can create benefit while design and terms impose unfair pressure.
No; one label must settle every effect.

questions.explanation: Stakeholder effects can be mixed and require evidence on terms and outcomes.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 2

questions.stem: Which ONE feature is central to Casas Bahia’s business model in the historical case?

options.text: A wholesale-only model with no direct relationship with household customers.
Interest-free grants funded entirely by charitable donations.
Credit-financed sales of household goods to customers often underserved by conventional banks.
Cash-only sales of unbranded essentials to customers with high regular salaries.
Exclusion of applicants who do not already own a conventional bank account.

questions.explanation: The case centres on providing credit-financed access to durable household goods for people often excluded from conventional banking.
questions.source: Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/5e297fec4bdc448582f4c676a562cf39) — Case pp. 10–11.

questions.stem: Which ONE statement about customer assessment is TRUE of the case?

options.text: Credit analysts were prohibited from asking about a customer’s circumstances.
Every applicant was accepted without any credit assessment.
The company relied only on a current account balance supplied by a bank.
Every customer without a prior bank loan was automatically rejected.
Credit analysts could use personal assessment where standard records or automated scoring did not settle an application.

questions.explanation: The case describes credit analysts making personal assessments when standard records or automated scoring were insufficient, rather than universal acceptance or rejection.
questions.source: Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/5e297fec4bdc448582f4c676a562cf39) — Case p. 11.

questions.stem: What commercial effect did requiring customers to make instalment payments in the stores have?

options.text: It supported ongoing relationships and created opportunities for cross-selling.
It removed the retailer’s need to maintain customer information.
It prevented customers from seeing other products while repaying.
It meant that the company could not encourage repeat purchases.
It guaranteed that credit purchases cost the same as cash purchases.

questions.explanation: In-store repayments maintained relationships and repeatedly exposed customers to products, giving the retailer opportunities to cross-sell.
questions.source: Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/5e297fec4bdc448582f4c676a562cf39) — Case pp. 12–13.

questions.stem: Which ONE observation in the case shows why low default is not a complete measure of customer welfare?

options.text: The company had no way to identify whether customers repaid.
The company refused to let customers visit the stores after their first purchase.
Customers were prevented from buying household goods on credit.
A customer described postponing replacement of damaged sandals in order to keep instalments up to date.
Every credit purchase was provided without interest or additional cost.

questions.explanation: The sandals example shows that timely repayment can involve foregoing other needs; low default therefore does not measure the whole welfare effect.
questions.source: Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/5e297fec4bdc448582f4c676a562cf39) — Case p. 12.

questions.stem: Which ONE comparison about default rates is consistent with the case?

options.text: Furniture had a lower default rate than portable items, with the ease of locating and recovering goods identified as relevant.
The case gives no connection between recovery of goods and repayment patterns.
Furniture had the highest default solely because it was installed in customers’ homes.
Portable items had no default because they were easier for the retailer to recover.
Default was identical across all product categories.

questions.explanation: The case links furniture’s lower default with being installed and more readily recovered, unlike portable items that were harder to monitor.
questions.source: Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/5e297fec4bdc448582f4c676a562cf39) — Case p. 12.

questions.stem: A customer can meet a small monthly instalment but does not compare the total credit cost with the cash price. Which ONE ethical concern is most directly raised?

options.text: Accepting a payment schedule proves full understanding of every alternative.
The ability to repay one instalment establishes that no other needs are displaced.
The retailer’s commercial success establishes that the customer receives the best possible deal.
A small instalment establishes that credit is costless.
Monthly affordability may obscure the total financing cost and its effect on the household budget.

questions.explanation: A manageable monthly payment does not reveal the full financing cost or what else the household must forgo. Informed comparison requires attention to both.
questions.source: Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/5e297fec4bdc448582f4c676a562cf39)

questions.stem: Which ONE interpretation of the 2002 debt pardon is supported by the original case?

options.text: It combined a tax deduction with a marketing opportunity to bring previously inactive or blacklisted customers back.
It had no financial or commercial advantage of any kind for the company.
It permanently prevented the affected customers from buying on credit again.
It forgave every future credit purchase for every customer indefinitely.
It was described as a government payment replacing the company’s lost revenue.

questions.explanation: The case describes the write-off as both tax-reducing and commercially useful in bringing customers back. It was not presented as having no business advantage.
questions.source: Casas Bahia — Marketing to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/5e297fec4bdc448582f4c676a562cf39) — Case p. 13; this tests the mechanism rather than repeating official sample 6.

chapters.title: Discussion Group 3: Food Engineering & Industry Science
chapters.description: Industry-funded research, product engineering and unequal responsibility.

questions.stem: What happened at the 1999 food-industry meeting described by Moss?

options.text: Government banned processed food.
Consumers set marketing standards.
A collective health response was proposed but rejected amid competitive concerns.
Firms agreed to end sugar use.

questions.explanation: The case illustrates a collective-action problem.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: How can a “healthier” snack label produce moral licensing?

options.text: Reformulation ends marketing.
Health claims are never informative.
Consumers may feel permitted to eat more, offsetting per-serving improvement.
Labels always reduce consumption.

questions.explanation: Total impact depends on behaviour as well as composition.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: Why was Coca-Cola’s baby-carrot example ethically important?

options.text: The same behavioural tools can promote a healthier product, so context and consequences matter.
Marketing methods are inherently evil.
Carrots and soft drinks are identical.
Transparency is irrelevant.

questions.explanation: Tools are not judged apart from product, audience and likely impact.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: How should responsibility be divided in engineered-food markets?

options.text: Unequally across consumers, firms and regulators according to knowledge, power and vulnerability.
Consumers alone are responsible.
Firms alone control every choice.
Responsibility must be numerically equal.

questions.explanation: Agency remains, but superior information and design power increase corporate duties.
questions.source: MG2008 Discussion Group 3; Reading 20; Michael Moss

questions.stem: Reading 20 — ILSI. Which ONE concern is central to the report on food policy?

options.text: Industry funding and institutional access can create conflicts of interest in research and public-health policy.
Non-profit status prevents an organisation from having any conflict of interest.
A scientific-sounding name establishes independence from commercial influence.
Industry participation is sufficient to prove that every individual study is false.
The presence of academics removes the need to examine funding or governance.

questions.explanation: Funding and access to policy institutions can create conflicts of interest. These concerns require examination without assuming every associated study is necessarily false.
questions.source: Reading 20 — Industry influence on global food policy (https://app.notion.com/p/87cf125993e24e7a931744dfaacbf228)

questions.stem: Which ONE method best fits the assigned ILSI critique?

options.text: Accept the website’s claims as sufficient because the organisation is a non-profit.
Use the presence of academic contributors as proof of complete independence.
Assess credibility by the scientific appearance of the name without investigating the organisation.
Reject every individual research finding solely because an industry participant is involved.
Compare the organisation’s self-presentation with independent evidence about funding, governance and influence.

questions.explanation: The assignment asks for a critique comparing self-presentation with other evidence. Funding, governance and influence are relevant; names and status alone are insufficient.
questions.source: MG2008 Third Discussion Group Details (https://app.notion.com/p/16190bbd702343a486f5766788627d7d); Reading 20 — Industry influence on global food policy (https://app.notion.com/p/87cf125993e24e7a931744dfaacbf228)

questions.stem: In Moss’s article, the “bliss point” principally refers to:

options.text: A legal limit requiring every product to contain no added sugar.
The lowest retail price at which all consumers can afford a product.
A sensory level that maximises liking, rather than an assumption that more sweetness is always better.
A measure proving that a product cannot be overconsumed.
The point at which consumers fully understand every long-term health effect.

questions.explanation: The bliss point is an optimum in liking; adding more sweetness beyond that point does not necessarily increase appeal.
questions.source: The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food (https://app.notion.com/p/96d680f65b69412ea61a030691ec9647)

questions.stem: In Moss’s account of “sensory-specific satiety”, which ONE statement is TRUE?

options.text: A strong, distinctive flavour can reduce the desire to continue eating, helping explain the commercial appeal of more complex formulations.
It measures whether the retail price makes a product affordable to all consumers.
Consumers become unable to distinguish flavours as soon as they have eaten one serving.
The concept establishes that every highly palatable product has no calories.
Increasing sweetness always increases liking at the same rate.

questions.explanation: Sensory-specific satiety describes reduced desire in response to a pronounced flavour. The article connects avoiding an overriding single flavour with continued consumption.
questions.source: The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food (https://app.notion.com/p/96d680f65b69412ea61a030691ec9647)

questions.stem: According to Moss’s discussion of Lunchables, marketing increasingly appealed to children through which ONE idea?

options.text: The view that parents’ time pressures played no role in developing the product.
The promise that every tray contained only unprocessed fresh ingredients.
The claim that children were uninterested in making choices about food.
The decision to stop using taste or convenience in the product’s positioning.
The feeling of control involved in choosing and assembling what they would eat.

questions.explanation: Moss describes positioning Lunchables around children’s feeling of choice and control, not only the physical contents of the tray.
questions.source: The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food (https://app.notion.com/p/96d680f65b69412ea61a030691ec9647); MG2008 Third Discussion Group Details (https://app.notion.com/p/16190bbd702343a486f5766788627d7d)

questions.stem: In the Cheetos discussion reported by Moss, “vanishing caloric density” refers to which ONE claim by the food scientist?

options.text: Consumers can infer a product’s full nutritional value from its texture alone.
The product’s price falls as more units are sold.
The food’s calories physically disappear when it is chewed.
Rapid melting in the mouth can make a food seem less calorific and encourage continued eating.
Every light-textured food contains less energy per gram than fresh fruit.

questions.explanation: The article reports the scientist’s claim that rapid melting can make a food seem less calorific and encourage eating. It does not mean the food’s calories disappear.
questions.source: The Extraordinary Science of Addictive Junk Food (https://app.notion.com/p/96d680f65b69412ea61a030691ec9647) — This tests the article’s reported account, not an independently verified clinical rule.

chapters.title: Week 7 — Greener Economies & Wellbeing (Pretty)
chapters.description: Reading-grounded applications of substitution, wellbeing pathways, meaningful attachment and cautious interpretation of historical health costs.

questions.stem: A government concludes from Pretty et al. that additional income never improves wellbeing. What is the best correction?

options.text: Income growth can meet basic needs at low income levels; the link becomes weaker in already affluent settings.
The paper argues that income has exactly the same wellbeing effect at every income level.
The paper claims that only possessions determine wellbeing.
The paper identifies a single income threshold that applies identically to every person.

questions.explanation: The argument distinguishes meeting basic needs from the weaker GDP–wellbeing relationship in affluent populations; it is not a claim that income never matters.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: A city adds green products to residents’ shopping without reducing other consumption. Why might this fall short of Pretty et al.’s proposal?

options.text: The proposal treats GDP growth as sufficient evidence that all externalities have fallen.
The proposal emphasises substituting sustainable goods and non-material activities for damaging material consumption.
The proposal rejects all purchases, including sustainable goods.
The proposal assumes that an environmental label eliminates the impact of any quantity bought.

questions.explanation: Substitution matters. Efficiency or greener products can be overtaken by growth in total consumption.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: Which choice best illustrates the paper’s sustainable behaviours involving non-material consumption?

options.text: Replacing every working household device with a new model each year.
Treating higher spending alone as evidence of improved community connections.
Replacing a shopping outing with a community walking and volunteering activity.
Buying additional short-lived products because their advertising uses natural imagery.

questions.explanation: The proposed behaviours include nature contact and community participation, not merely purchasing products presented as green.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: A neighbourhood walking group improves activity, nature contact and social ties together. How does this fit Pretty et al.’s model?

options.text: Each activity must be assigned to exactly one pathway with no overlaps.
Community ties count only if participants buy products.
Only an increase in GDP can connect these outcomes.
One activity can support several interacting wellbeing pathways.

questions.explanation: The six factors interact. Nature-based social activity can improve several at once, which is also why health-cost categories can overlap.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: A local project builds networks, reciprocity and trust among neighbours. Which asset in Pretty et al.’s framework is most directly being strengthened?

options.text: The turnover rate of disposable goods.
Social capital.
Only physical inventory.
Only financial capital measured by sales revenue.

questions.explanation: The paper treats networks, shared norms, reciprocity and trust as social capital, with potential wellbeing benefits.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: Why does the paper discuss positive countertrends alongside negative consumption externalities?

options.text: To argue that gardening and volunteering have no possible benefits.
To replace analysis of health effects with product-sales totals.
To recognise beneficial developments without assuming that they have reversed the overall adverse patterns.
To establish that every negative trend is statistically cancelled by one positive trend.

questions.explanation: Examples such as allotments, walking groups and recycling complicate the picture, but the authors do not conclude that all adverse aggregate trends have disappeared.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: The paper reduces its combined historical health-cost estimate to allow for overlap. What is the methodological reason?

options.text: All costs should be removed whenever a condition has several causes.
A cost reported by the NHS can never also matter to the wider economy.
The adjustment proves that the conditions are statistically independent.
The same person or treatment cost may appear under more than one condition.

questions.explanation: Comorbidity and interactive causes create double-counting risks. The reduction is an assumption to address overlap, not proof of precise causal attribution.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: How should a student use the paper’s UK health-cost figures in a current Irish policy discussion?

options.text: As historical, context-specific estimates requiring scrutiny, not as current Irish savings guaranteed by an intervention.
As exact current Irish costs because the conditions have the same names.
As proof that every pound of the estimated burden is immediately avoidable.
As a measured return from one nationwide randomised policy trial.

questions.explanation: The paper combines historical UK estimates with assumptions about overlap. Estimated burden is not identical to the achievable savings of a particular policy.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: Which policy best reflects the paper’s emphasis on prevention and environmental context?

options.text: Require individuals to be active while removing safe walking access.
Create accessible green walking routes and support community activities before ill-health develops.
Wait for illness and treat it without considering living conditions.
Measure wellbeing solely by spending on treatment.

questions.explanation: The authors argue for enabling healthier behaviour through social and environmental conditions, not relying solely on treatment or individual exhortation.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 10: Pretty et al. (2016), “Improving health and well-being independently of GDP”, original PDF, article pp. 11–30.

questions.stem: Reading 10 — Pretty et al. Which ONE example best captures “cathexis” as discussed in relation to possessions and wellbeing?

options.text: Increasing consumption primarily to maintain rank relative to other consumers.
Measuring an object’s value solely by its resale price.
Assuming that buying a greener product cancels every impact of additional consumption.
Replacing a serviceable object whenever a newer model becomes available.
Valuing and caring for an object because of the emotional meaning attached to it.

questions.explanation: Cathexis is emotional investment in a possession. It can make an object meaningful and worth caring for rather than replacing simply for novelty.
questions.source: Reading 10 — Improving wellbeing independently of GDP (https://app.notion.com/p/30736b7a0038414db8248afd771e2c36)

chapters.title: Week 7 — Marketing, Consumer Society & Hedonism
chapters.description: Critical reading of the facilitator argument, active consumers, psychological obsolescence and evidence limitations.

questions.stem: A critic describes advertising as injecting desires into passive consumers. What response most closely matches the reading?

options.text: Consumers always resist all advertising successfully.
Every purchase is a reflex with no interpretation.
Only marketers can attach meanings to products.
Consumers can filter, interpret and negotiate marketing meanings rather than simply absorb them.

questions.explanation: The authors favour a more active, negotiated account over a simple hypodermic stimulus–response model. This does not imply zero marketing influence.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: Why would equating marketing solely with advertising weaken an analysis of the reading?

options.text: Marketing also includes identifying segments, shaping offerings and making them available.
Advertising is unrelated to marketing in every circumstance.
The reading defines marketing solely as setting factory wages.
The reading argues that distribution choices never affect consumers.

questions.explanation: The account includes market selection, product offerings, availability and communication, among other decisions; promotion is only part of it.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: A working phone is discarded because promotion makes the newer model seem socially necessary. Which criticism does the reading acknowledge?

options.text: Material possessions cannot carry social meanings.
Psychological obsolescence can encourage replacement of serviceable products.
Functional breakdown is the only possible cause of replacement.
Every new model necessarily reduces waste.

questions.explanation: The authors acknowledge waste and the role of marketing in celebrating newer models, even while disputing that marketing created consumerism.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: An effective campaign discourages smoking. How does this example function in the authors’ argument?

options.text: Health campaigns prove that commercial promotion has no costs.
A beneficial campaign means audiences have no agency.
Marketing techniques can also be used to oppose consumption habits.
Any campaign using persuasion must increase total smoking.

questions.explanation: The reading treats marketing as a set of techniques that can serve different purposes, including reducing consumption, rather than as inherently consumption-increasing.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: What qualification do the authors make about the evidential strength of their paper?

options.text: They report a controlled experiment proving advertising never changes behaviour.
They calculate an exact share of consumerism caused by each advertisement.
They claim the concepts are straightforward to measure without empirical inquiry.
They acknowledge the absence of relevant data and the difficulty of measuring key concepts.

questions.explanation: The conclusion identifies a lack of relevant data and measurement challenges. The argument should not be presented as decisive experimental proof.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: A student argues that because materialism existed before modern advertising, advertising cannot intensify it. What is the best evaluation?

options.text: Earlier materialism challenges a claim that advertising invented it, but does not rule out later influence.
Historical precedence proves that advertising has no effect.
Materialism’s earlier existence proves modern advertising caused that earlier materialism.
The timing of materialism is irrelevant to a claim about its invention.

questions.explanation: Distinguish origin from reinforcement. The authors’ facilitator argument is compatible with acknowledging influence and psychological obsolescence.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: Which paired interpretation best compares Pretty et al. with the marketing reading?

options.text: Both papers use the same experiment to show that income never matters.
Pretty et al. examine consumption’s wellbeing costs and alternatives; the marketing authors challenge a simple account blaming marketing for originating consumerism.
Both papers establish that marketing alone explains all health problems.
Pretty et al. reject all benefits of material consumption, while the marketing authors reject all costs.

questions.explanation: The texts address related issues from different angles. Neither requires denying all benefits or all costs of consumption.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 11: O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy, “Marketing, the consumer society and hedonism”, original PDF, especially printed pp. 525, 543–545.

questions.stem: Reading 11 — O’Shaughnessy and O’Shaughnessy. Which ONE account best represents the authors’ conclusion about marketing and consumerism?

options.text: Marketing created materialism from nothing in societies that previously had no such desires.
The costs of consumer society establish that it provides no convenience or freedom of choice.
Marketing has acted more as a facilitator than as the sole manufacturer of consumerism.
Consumers passively accept marketing messages without interpretation or resistance.
The authors conclude that marketing has no influence on consumption patterns.

questions.explanation: The authors conclude that marketing has been more facilitator than manufacturer of consumerism; they do not describe consumers as wholly passive or deny marketing any influence.
questions.source: Reading 11 — Marketing, consumer society and hedonism (https://app.notion.com/p/1a5f0ac880ef4da7b864a10a7f075815) — Conclusion, article p. 544 / PDF p. 21.

chapters.title: Week 7 — TOMS, Aid Effectiveness & Recipient Agency
chapters.description: Separate charitable intent and output from outcomes, cost-effectiveness, comparative evidence and recipient agency.

questions.stem: A company cites the number of shoes donated as proof that children’s educational outcomes improved. Which distinction is missing?

options.text: Higher shoe sales automatically measure school attendance.
An outcome is simply another name for the quantity distributed.
An output delivered is not the same as an outcome achieved.
Donations cannot be counted under any circumstances.

questions.explanation: Counting shoes establishes an activity or output. Educational benefit requires evidence about outcomes such as attendance.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Which statement accurately reflects the shoe-donation findings reported in the TOMS reading?

options.text: Every measured outcome improved dramatically.
No child used or valued the shoes.
The study proved that shoe donations destroyed every local business.
Children liked and used the shoes, but no significant improvement in school attendance or self-esteem was found.

questions.explanation: The account distinguishes some use and enjoyment from the absence of significant improvements on the highlighted wider outcomes.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: What is the key untested assumption when a campaign claims that giving girls a particular consumer item will resolve school absence?

options.text: That lack of the item is the decisive barrier, rather than other constraints such as facilities or pain.
That schools and families can have any influence on attendance.
That the item can be physically distributed.
That all charitable activity must be commercial.

questions.explanation: The reading warns against jumping from an observed hardship to a presumed single material cause and solution.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Why does the TOMS reading propose considering cash transfers as a comparator?

options.text: Recipient choice is irrelevant once donors have good intentions.
Recipients may have information about their own priorities that an outside donor lacks.
Cash is proven superior to every good or service in every context.
The original TOMS evaluation randomly compared shoes with cash and settled the question.

questions.explanation: Cash can allow recipients to choose among needs. The reading explicitly says TOMS had not run a comparable cash-versus-own-programme study and does not claim cash always wins.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: A campaign depicts recipients as helpless people awaiting rescue by shoppers. What ethical concern is most directly raised?

options.text: It proves that the product cannot be sold at a profit.
It means no buyer can have genuinely charitable motives.
It can diminish recipient agency and reinforce a paternalistic view of poverty.
It gives recipients too much control over the programme design.

questions.explanation: The critique targets a donor-centred story that sidelines recipients’ knowledge and agency, not a claim that all buyers have bad intentions.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: How does the appended commentary qualify the strongest criticism of TOMS’ effects on local shoe markets?

options.text: It proves every local shoe vendor permanently closed.
It reports that market effects were never considered.
It establishes that all imported donations increase local sales.
It describes a small negative effect, not wholesale destruction of local markets.

questions.explanation: The commentary reports some displacement of local sales but characterises the effect as small. Avoid turning that into an unsupported claim of destroyed markets.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Which organisational response in the appended TOMS commentary is most consistent with evidence-based responsibility?

options.text: Commission evaluation, disclose findings and adapt the intervention to recipients’ needs.
Treat good intentions as sufficient reason to avoid evaluation.
Suppress disappointing findings to preserve the campaign’s image.
Count only sales growth when assessing recipient wellbeing.

questions.explanation: The appended researcher praises transparency, willingness to evaluate and changes in shoe type and programme design. The case is not a uniformly negative judgement of the organisation.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Why might directly providing a good still be justified in some contexts, according to the TOMS reading?

options.text: A community benefit guarantees that any chosen product is cost-effective.
Some interventions, such as vaccinations, can generate benefits beyond the individual recipient.
Cash has been shown to fail in every poverty programme.
Donors always know more about every need than recipients.

questions.explanation: The reading gives community-wide benefits as one reason direct provision might make sense. It still calls for comparison and evidence, not a blanket rule.
questions.source: MG2008 Reading 12: Amanda Taub (2015), “Buying TOMS shoes is a terrible way to help poor people”, and appended Wydick commentary, original supplied DOCX.

questions.stem: Which option gives the COMPLETE set of commercial arguments for responsible conduct discussed in the lecture? (i) Retaining customers and employees; (ii) maintaining community support and a social licence to operate; (iii) managing risk and uncertainty.

options.text: (i) and (ii) only.
(ii) only.
(i), (ii) and (iii).
(i) and (iii) only.
(ii) and (iii) only.

questions.explanation: Retention, a social licence to operate and risk management are all commercial arguments for responsible conduct; they explain potential business benefits rather than proving a duty-based motive.
questions.source: Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8135a529c4c28c26f9c1)

questions.stem: Which ONE argument for corporate responsibility is a moral argument rather than merely a business-case argument?

options.text: Responsible conduct can help retain commercially valuable customers.
A positive reputation can make recruiting skilled employees easier.
A company should address harms for which it bears responsibility even where doing so offers no competitive advantage.
Lower material waste can reduce a company’s production costs.
Community approval can reduce obstacles to a company’s operations.

questions.explanation: The moral argument concerns responsibility for harm even without a competitive payoff. The other options describe commercial benefits.
questions.source: Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8135a529c4c28c26f9c1)

questions.stem: A company offers employee housing, but workers would risk losing both their income and accommodation if they challenge management. Which ONE interpretation best fits the lecture’s discussion?

options.text: The housing arrangement has no ethical relevance because it lies outside wages.
The existence of a benefit establishes that the employment relationship is ethically satisfactory.
A benefit can improve living conditions while also creating dependency and unequal power.
An employee’s initial acceptance removes every later concern about bargaining power.
The possibility of dependency proves that all employer-provided benefits should be abolished.

questions.explanation: Employer-provided housing can provide a real benefit and also increase dependency, especially where challenging management threatens both income and shelter.
questions.source: Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8135a529c4c28c26f9c1)

questions.stem: Which ONE interpretation is consistent with the module’s discussion of consumerism?

options.text: Every increase in consumption necessarily produces an equal increase in subjective wellbeing.
Consumer choice proves that marketing cannot influence the pattern of demand.
The existence of material comfort removes the possibility of harmful consumption.
Criticism of consumerism requires denying that any purchased good can improve life.
Consumption may provide convenience and choice while also contributing to waste and status-driven dissatisfaction.

questions.explanation: A balanced account recognises both the conveniences of consumption and its possible social and environmental costs, rather than treating either side as exhaustive.
questions.source: Lecture 7 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c8135a529c4c28c26f9c1); Reading 11 — Marketing, consumer society and hedonism (https://app.notion.com/p/1a5f0ac880ef4da7b864a10a7f075815)

chapters.title: Week 8 — Degrowth & Bottom of the Pyramid

questions.stem: Which option gives the COMPLETE set of practices consistent with the lecture’s broader degrowth discussion? (i) Sharing resources and supporting commons; (ii) recognising care and non-market activity; (iii) pursuing status through ever-higher material consumption.

options.text: (ii) only.
(i) and (iii) only.
(i), (ii) and (iii).
(i) and (ii) only.
(iii) only.

questions.explanation: Sharing, commons and care fit the broader degrowth discussion; escalating material consumption to pursue status does not.
questions.source: Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81cb9c22c1d8e33ac96e)

questions.stem: Why does the lecture distinguish affluent consumption from consumption by people with unmet basic needs?

options.text: The existence of poverty establishes that total consumption can grow without environmental constraints.
Every purchase by a low-income household is necessarily a basic need.
Affluent consumers have no responsibility for resource use because markets reflect demand.
The same proportional reduction in consumption has identical consequences at every income level.
Reducing excess in affluent settings need not imply denying essential goods and opportunities to low-income groups.

questions.explanation: The lecture distinguishes reducing affluent excess from meeting unmet needs. An identical consumption cut can have very different effects at different income levels.
questions.source: Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81cb9c22c1d8e33ac96e)

questions.stem: If all households spend more in an effort to improve their position relative to one another, which ONE issue arises?

options.text: The resulting demand has no connection to resource consumption.
Every household must move upward in the status ranking by the same amount.
Relative position necessarily improves whenever absolute spending rises.
Material spending can increase without everyone improving their relative status.
A status comparison measures the same thing as the satisfaction of an unmet basic need.

questions.explanation: Relative status is comparative: everyone spending more does not mean everyone rises relative to everyone else.
questions.source: Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81cb9c22c1d8e33ac96e)

questions.stem: Which ONE commercial logic is central to the pro-BOP approach discussed in class?

options.text: Products should be designed for affluent markets and sold unchanged regardless of local conditions.
Low individual incomes mean that no commercially viable market can exist.
Large numbers of customers and suitable low-cost models can make low-margin transactions commercially attractive.
Commercial sales to poor customers establish poverty reduction without any further evidence.
Low margins eliminate the need to consider distribution and transaction costs.

questions.explanation: The pro-BOP model can combine small margins with large numbers of customers, but requires suitable cost and distribution models and does not itself prove development impact.
questions.source: Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81cb9c22c1d8e33ac96e); Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/0664576fcbac4293864507bc52d752a6)

questions.stem: A washing machine is adapted for unreliable infrastructure through features such as protection against power problems and flexible water filling. What principle does this illustrate?

options.text: Design should respond to the conditions in which customers will actually use the product.
Lower-income customers necessarily prefer fewer useful functions regardless of context.
The availability of an appliance guarantees a particular household income increase.
A standard affluent-market product can always be transferred unchanged.
Customers’ local infrastructure is separate from the value of the product.

questions.explanation: Product design must fit actual infrastructure and use conditions. Adaptation can make a product useful without guaranteeing a particular income outcome.
questions.source: Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81cb9c22c1d8e33ac96e)

questions.stem: The mobile-money example discussed in Lecture 8 principally illustrates:

options.text: Providing charitable grants that recipients never have to exchange or collect.
Requiring every sender and recipient to own a smartphone and a conventional bank account.
Using local agents and basic mobile-phone access to make money transfers available without relying on conventional bank access.
Replacing all cash handling with a system that has no local agents.
Eliminating all transaction costs merely by using a mobile network.

questions.explanation: The mobile-money example uses local agents and mobile access to enable transfers where conventional banking access is limited; it does not require smartphones for everyone.
questions.source: Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81cb9c22c1d8e33ac96e)

questions.stem: Which ONE conclusion best avoids romanticising the recycling activity discussed in relation to Dharavi?

options.text: Recycling revenue removes the need to examine health and safety.
Poor living conditions establish that residents perform no economically valuable activity.
Informal enterprise and hazardous work cannot occur in the same place.
The existence of profitable recycling establishes that working conditions are satisfactory.
Economic value and entrepreneurial activity can coexist with hazardous work and poor living conditions.

questions.explanation: Economic activity and entrepreneurial effort can coexist with serious hazards. Neither romanticising poverty nor denying residents’ economic contribution is justified.
questions.source: Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81cb9c22c1d8e33ac96e)

questions.stem: Which ONE comparison most accurately distinguishes Karnani’s critique from a simple consumer-market version of the BOP argument?

options.text: The debate concerns advertising style only, rather than income, production or welfare.
Karnani treats every low-price consumer product as sufficient evidence of poverty reduction.
Karnani emphasises poor people’s role as producers and the need to raise real incomes, rather than treating sales alone as poverty reduction.
The pro-BOP argument requires that poor people be excluded from markets.
Karnani argues that the private sector can have no role in improving poor people’s lives.

questions.explanation: Karnani’s critique shifts attention to production and real income. Selling goods profitably and reducing poverty are different claims.
questions.source: Lecture 8 — original recording/transcript (https://app.notion.com/p/3adba34e944c81cb9c22c1d8e33ac96e); Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/0664576fcbac4293864507bc52d752a6); Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid (https://app.notion.com/p/f5a771195d8f440aa7b798b9592052cf)

questions.stem: Reading 1 — Penneys. Which ONE observation best expresses the ethics–price paradox discussed in the reading?

options.text: A supplier code establishes that all factory conditions meet the stated standard.
Expressing concern guarantees a sustained change in purchasing behaviour.
Consumers can express concern about production ethics while continuing to buy mainly on price.
Low prices demonstrate that consumers have no ethical concerns.
A purchase reveals every factor the consumer considered and the weight attached to each.

questions.explanation: The Penneys reading highlights a gap between stated ethical concern and price-driven purchasing; expressed attitudes do not guarantee sustained behavioural change.
questions.source: Reading 1 — Penneys: ethics–price paradox (https://app.notion.com/p/709ddc600497481299913782587692c9)

questions.stem: Reading 4 — Evaluating ethics in practice. What does the Wells Fargo example suggest should accompany analysis of individual employees’ choices?

options.text: A conclusion that applying a named ethical theory removes the need for case evidence.
A presumption that commercial success validates the practices used to achieve it.
A focus on external advertising while excluding internal targets.
Examination of managerial pressures, incentives and organisational culture.
An assumption that all employee decisions are isolated from the organisation.

questions.explanation: The Wells Fargo discussion connects individual decisions with targets, managerial pressure and organisational culture, rather than treating them as isolated choices.
questions.source: Reading 4 — Evaluating business ethics in practice (https://app.notion.com/p/e6517b09614a415fa762790025f1868d)

questions.stem: Reading 5 — OpenStax pp. 44–53. Which ONE contrast between utilitarian and Kantian reasoning is correct?

options.text: The two approaches differ only in terminology and must recommend the same action.
Kantian reasoning treats a profitable result as sufficient to establish a duty-based motive.
Both approaches define the right action solely by the executive’s private financial return.
Utilitarianism excludes the consequences for people other than the decision-maker.
Utilitarianism assesses consequences for overall utility; Kantian reasoning gives a central role to duty and the basis of action.

questions.explanation: Utilitarian reasoning centres on overall consequences; Kantian reasoning centres on duty and the basis of action. The two need not give identical recommendations.
questions.source: Reading 5 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 44–53) (https://app.notion.com/p/cf51b12e0511479e8bde7062374f8a59)

questions.stem: Reading 6 — OpenStax pp. 54–58. A person dividing a cake does not know which slice they will receive. What feature of fair decision-making does this exercise illustrate?

options.text: Existing property holdings determine the only permissible principles of distribution.
Equal basic liberties must be traded away whenever aggregate output increases.
Fairness can be assessed without considering how the decision affects different positions.
The divider should first secure the largest share and then justify the allocation.
Not knowing one’s eventual position can discourage designing the arrangement solely for personal advantage.

questions.explanation: Uncertainty about which share one receives can discourage self-serving allocation and illustrates the logic of impartial choice.
questions.source: Reading 6 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 54–58) (https://app.notion.com/p/d61a87e18e554146a2931313adc789dd)

questions.stem: Reading 8 — Food warnings. Which option gives the COMPLETE set of campaigners’ proposals among these? (i) Warning labels; (ii) salt-related taxes; (iii) restrictions on junk-food marketing or sports sponsorship.

options.text: (i) only.
(i), (ii) and (iii).
(i) and (iii) only.
(ii) and (iii) only.
(i) and (ii) only.

questions.explanation: The reading reports all three as campaign proposals. Reporting a proposal is not the same as saying it has become law.
questions.source: Reading 8 — Warning labels on everyday food (https://app.notion.com/p/ec291f7c194c40baa2d7ced9de445b83) — These are reported proposals, not a claim that all were enacted.

questions.stem: Reading 9 — OpenStax pp. 67–82. A group recognises a problem affecting it but has not yet organised to act. In the reading’s classification of publics, this group is:

options.text: An active public.
An aware public.
A latent public.
An enabling stakeholder by definition.
A nonpublic.

questions.explanation: An aware public recognises a problem but has not yet organised action. A latent public does not recognise it; an active public has begun to organise.
questions.source: Reading 9 — Business Ethics Textbook (pp. 67–82) (https://app.notion.com/p/13887a7ef2e74bb5b5408a63c25fb373)

questions.stem: Reading 13 — Hammond and Prahalad. The e-Choupal example is used to illustrate which ONE potential contribution of business?

options.text: Guaranteeing that every commercial transaction with a poor person eliminates poverty.
Improving producers’ access to information and markets in ways that can combine economic opportunity with inclusion.
Excluding low-income groups from market participation until they become affluent.
Removing producers’ ability to compare prices so that transactions become faster.
Substituting product advertising for any change in information or distribution.

questions.explanation: The e-Choupal example concerns information and market access for producers, illustrating a possible commercial contribution to economic inclusion.
questions.source: Reading 13 — Selling to the Poor (https://app.notion.com/p/0664576fcbac4293864507bc52d752a6)

questions.stem: Reading 14 — Karnani. Which ONE conclusion would he most strongly challenge?

options.text: Growth in sales to poor consumers is, by itself, sufficient evidence that poverty has been reduced.
Poor people should be considered as producers as well as consumers.
Increasing poor people’s real income is important to poverty reduction.
A profitable opportunity and a development outcome are distinct claims requiring evidence.
The unit cost of small packages matters when assessing value.

questions.explanation: Karnani challenges treating consumer sales as sufficient evidence of poverty reduction; real income and productive opportunities must also be assessed.
questions.source: Reading 14 — The mirage of marketing to the Bottom of the Pyramid (https://app.notion.com/p/f5a771195d8f440aa7b798b9592052cf)

questions.stem: Reading 16 — Kiva. Which ONE statement correctly distinguishes the lender-facing description from borrowers’ possible costs?

options.text: Kiva not charging interest directly does not mean that partner microfinance institutions charge borrowers no interest.
The absence of a lender return establishes that the borrower faces no fees or financing cost.
A personal borrower story establishes the exact welfare effect of the loan.
A non-profit intermediary’s status prevents every partner from charging interest.
Every amount supplied through the platform is a gift rather than a repayable loan.

questions.explanation: Borrower cost depends on partner institutions’ terms as well as the platform’s own model. No direct interest charged by Kiva does not imply a free loan for the borrower.
questions.source: Reading 16 — Criticisms of Kiva (https://app.notion.com/p/50c2ee2ea3c24a289206328cec48b40a)

questions.stem: Reading 17 — Nestlé. Which ONE interpretation of the reported forced-labour disclosure in the Thai seafood supply chain is most defensible?

options.text: Disclosure can be significant while still leaving questions about hidden risks and effective remediation.
Only final consumers have responsibilities for the disclosed conditions.
A disclosure in one supply chain resolves every controversy involving the company.
Admitting a problem proves that every supplier has already remedied it.
The existence of a disclosure establishes that no further independent scrutiny is needed.

questions.explanation: Disclosure can be important without establishing that every problem is solved. Risk identification and effective remediation remain separate questions.
questions.source: Reading 17 — Nestlé: corporate conduct and responsibility (https://app.notion.com/p/0c49665110ee4c1ea74b14dd2d954c5f)

questions.stem: Reading 18 — KitKat. Which ONE statement preserves the distinction between the certification arrangements discussed?

options.text: All certification schemes necessarily provide the same price floor and premium.
The article concerns packaging design rather than terms affecting cocoa producers.
Using another certification means the company has stopped using any external scheme.
Fairtrade’s minimum-price and premium arrangements cannot simply be assumed to be identical to the terms of Rainforest Alliance certification.
A change in certification guarantees that every producer’s income will increase.

questions.explanation: Fairtrade’s floor-price and premium arrangements cannot be assumed to match the terms of another certification. A changed label does not itself establish a producer income gain.
questions.source: Reading 18 — KitKat ends Fairtrade link (https://app.notion.com/p/70a8753a79c74e1895a0b78e8014a3ed)

questions.stem: Reading 19 — Big Oil and plastics. What strategy does the report describe?

options.text: A verified worldwide end to fossil-fuel companies’ involvement in plastic production.
Industry lobbying to influence trade negotiations and weaken Kenya’s restrictions on plastics and waste imports.
A completed agreement guaranteeing that all imported plastic would be recycled safely.
A campaign to exclude industry interests from international trade negotiations.
A requirement that every exporting company remove all packaging from its products.

questions.explanation: The article reports lobbying around trade negotiations and Kenyan plastics restrictions, not a verified guarantee of safe recycling or the end of plastic production.
questions.source: Reading 19 — Big Oil looks to flood Africa with plastic (https://app.notion.com/p/77374bff8d26443eb9712c47574dd788)

questions.stem: Reading 21 — Pringles and Subway. Which ONE conclusion would be INCORRECT?

options.text: A court’s reasoning should be read in its legal context.
A product’s marketing description does not necessarily determine its tax classification.
A favourable food classification for tax purposes establishes that the product is nutritionally healthy.
A tax decision can depend on the particular statutory definition at issue.
A legal category and a nutritional evaluation need not answer the same question.

questions.explanation: Tax categories answer a particular legal question; they do not by themselves establish a product’s healthfulness or settle all marketing claims.
questions.source: Reading 21 — Pringles and Subway VAT rulings (https://app.notion.com/p/fc932f86976d4c78b29aa6f4b72d6152)
